YARMOUTH-BAR HARBOR    ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION OF VESSEL
speechtext:
In November, 1950, Mr. Speaker, I made an announcement that the lack of steel had made it necessary for the government to suspend temporarily construction of the proposed Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry. Today I am happy to inform the house that the government has reviewed the situation with respect to availability of scarce materials and, on the advice of the Canadian maritime commission, and after consultation with the premier of Nova Scotia has agreed that tenders should now be invited for the construction of the vessel.
I should like to remind the house that the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry project is not only a federal-provincial project, it is an international project including as it does the construction of approaches, causeway, pierhead and terminal facilities by the state of Maine and the town of Bar Harbor. I am happy to say that the Maine legislature has passed, and the governor has signed, the legislative bill relating to this work.
May I say a word or two about the ship itself? The vessel will have an over-all length of 348 feet; breadth at main deck 65 feet; car capacity 150 automobiles; total passengers carried 600. There are two car decks, the lower car deck having head clearance for long-distance refrigerated trailer trucks and buses. The service speed of the vessel will be approximately 18J knots. A notable feature of the vessel's construction is that it will be equipped with a Denny-Brown stabilizer which has the effect of minimizing vesselrolling during rough weather. In the summer tourist season the ship is scheduled to make the round-trip voyage in daylight hours. Our Nova Scotia members can readily appreciate the value of such a unit.
While initially the ferry will be dependent on summer tourist traffic, the real justification for the vessel is the hope that having furnished this new gateway there will develop a commercial business by truck which will bring the produce of Nova Scotia to the markets of the United States and vice
versa. The ship, in reality, will be a continuation of the highway between Maine and Nova Scotia, along which will flow countless automobiles with passengers anxious to visit and admire the beauties of Nova Scotia and of the New England coast line.
I think that in fairness, Mr. Speaker, I should add that the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk) has been pressing me for a statement on this subject for the last two days. I have suggested to him that he not ask a question in the house concerning it because I hoped to be able to make a statement. I am sorry it was not possible to do so before this morning.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to the protest which this government sent a few weeks ago to the state department of the United States with regard to the transfer of one company of our 25th brigade to temporary guard duty on Koje island.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs advised the house that the government of the United States had accepted our protest. I believe that was the obvious thing for the government of the United States to do, because they had no alternative. They know perfectly well that a formal, publicized rejection of our protest would simply give the communist propaganda machine more material to use against us. In sending that protest I believe that we have already given them far too much of that kind of material.
I believe that the fact that the United States accepted our protest in no way excuses or justifies the great amount of publicity that attended the sending of that protest. If a government which has reached adult stature in the handling of external affairs wishes to send a protest to an allied government with regard to some matter, I believe that it does so in a quiet, restrained and unpublicized manner.
The only explanation which I can find for this tremendous amount of publicity is that the publicity machines in some of our departments of government are getting a little bit out of hand. First of all, we see the Department of National Health and Welfare flooding the country with pamphlets advertising the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Then in answer to that move we see the Department of External Affairs counter with
Supply-External Affairs headline publicity in which their minister is portrayed as the great white father who fights the battles of all Canadians outside of our shores.
It is going to be very interesting to see what the Department of Finance and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration are going to be able to do in order to further boost their ministers in the leadership race as it draws close to the line.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we have a look at the circumstances which have prompted this very unfortunate outburst on the part of our government. The circumstances are these: One company of our 25th brigade was sent by the United Nations commander to share in the police duties on Koje island. This was a temporary assignment, within the theatre of operations, and one which the United Nations commander was quite entitled to make.
His only obligation was first to get in touch with the commander of the British commonwealth division, under whose command our 25th brigade has been for some time, and request that the company should be sent. However, despite this fact, the government sent to the state department of the United States a protest which unfortunately received a great deal of headline publicity.
If this assignment was to have been a permanent one, or if our troops were to be sent outside the theatre of operations, then I believe this protest would have been justified, provided that the United Nations commander had not first received the permission of the Canadian government. However, to send a much publicized protest to the state department because of a temporary assignment, within the theatre of operations, and which was merely to do our share of the police duty necessary on Koje island, does, I feel, Mr. Chairman, make us look rather ridiculous in the eyes of our allies.
It has, I believe, shown a complete lack of understanding of the need of a field commander to feel free to assign troops under his command to normal duties, of a temporary nature, and within the theatre of operations.
I feel sure that during the last war there were many questions of allied policy on which Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Churchill were not in complete agreement, but the public was never aware of these differences. These statesmen knew that nothing feeds the enemy propaganda machine quite so well as to publicize differences between allies, and so they resolved their differences privately.
In conclusion, I say that I sincerely hope this government will learn from these two great statesmen, and when it feels called

Supply-External Affairs upon to criticize the action of an allied government in the future, it will do so in a restrained, dignified and unpublicized manner.

I happen to be the minister of the department which possesses what has been called this publicity machine, which I think consists of a press officer. I am glad to take the responsibility for anything that is done by my department.
The matter that has been referred to need not I think be exaggerated. Our statement, which was made in this house-because when we have important statements to make on matters of direct concern to Canadian interests I think it is desirable to make them in the House of Commons-indicated that we had sent a note, which has been called a note of protest. In fact it was a note expressing our concern that a detachment of Canadian soldiers had been removed from the brigade for duty elsewhere in Korea in circumstances which we thought at that time were such as to make possible prior consultation with the government. But it will be recalled by the committee that in the note we made it quite clear that military considerations must govern these matters, and that in a case of military emergency no formation should expect to operate as a formation if it is necessary to break it up. That exception is understood by us, and I am sure by other governments with forces in Korea. However, when our brigade was sent to Korea its directive in

this matter was quite clear. That directive, which was sent to the brigade commander and also to the unified command, was to the effect that the principle of the separate entity of the Canadian forces should at all times be maintained. That is a principle which has been considered of importance to Canadian governments from the time of the first war, and it was laid down in regard to our operations in Korea.
It was considered proper at this time to call attention to that principle, of course always excepting military emergency. That was done. The United States government has expressed its appreciation and understanding of the importance of this principle for us, and at the same time has quite rightly emphasized the overriding importance of military considerations. I think that this exchange of correspondence between the two governments has served a useful purpose, and I do not think that the communists are going to be able to exploit it to any great extent.
As I indicated in my statement, we are happy to have our brigade in Korea take its full share of duty there as a unit of the United Nations forces. That is a principle by which we are also governed. But, subject always to military considerations, we feel it important to make quite clear that the directive which was given to the brigade at the time, namely, that a separate entity should be maintained, should be observed not only in Korea but wherever Canadian troops are serving, because we have learned from experience that that is the best way that Canadian soldiers operate in campaigns outside of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on at least tour occasions in recent weeks members of this group have asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs for a statement respecting the attitude of the Canadian government toward the activities of Syngman Rhee. On several, indeed if not on all those occasions, the reply of the minister was that he would prefer to wait until we reached the discussion of his estimates, at which time he would be prepared to make a statement in the matter.
I might remind him that the first time I put a question to him regarding this matter was prior to the occasion when several of the united nations associated in the effort in Korea, indicated their dissatisfaction with Syngman Rhee's disregard of democratic practices. We had hoped that Canada might take the lead in connection with the matter.
At any rate the whole question is very much in the news these days. Almost every day there is an item of significant importance in news broadcasts as to the way in which Syngman Rhee is trying to get rid of any political opposition in that country.
I should like to take a moment to read to the committee an extract or two from the Christian Science Monitor of June 18, 1952, in which the chief far eastern correspondent of that paper, Mr. Henry S. Hayward, sets out some of the background. He says:
The "communist conspiracy" which President Rhee charges is behind the current South Korean political tempest is largely fictitious.
The "conspiracy" was conjured up, in other words, to justify the president's action in declaring a state of martial law, in arresting a dozen members of the national assembly, and in seizing emergency political powers.
Mr. Hayward points out that this article is based largely upon an interview he had with Mr. Paul F. Douglass, who is in Korea as one of Mr. Rhee's top political advisers. Having pointed that out, the writer of the article goes on to say:
Claims that a communist conspiracy exists among members of the national assembly with whom Mr. Rhee is feuding, that the assemblymen have accepted bribes, and that an increase in guerrilla activity threatens South Korea's security-all these are trumped-up charges manufactured to disguise or justify the declaration of martial law, the arrest and intimidation of assemblymen, and the grasping of emergency powers that will permit Mr. Rhee to remain in command, Mr. Douglass explains.
Obviously my reason for reading a few sentences from the Christian Science Monitor is because of the reputation that paper has for objective reporting on matters of this kind. As my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East, my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I have indicated on previous occasions, we feel that this is a matter of great concern to us. We knew when we went into the situation in Korea
Supply-External Affairs that we were not going to the defence of a well-organized and properly functioning democracy. We knew that we went in to take a stand against aggression. But I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs must agree with us that it is a pretty hard pill to swallow when we see that we would appear to be defending a regime that is engaging in such undemocratic processes, as is indicated in the news every day. I would hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would now be ready to state the views of the Canadian government in this matter.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is quite true that I did indicate on previous occasions that during the discussion of my estimates I would make known our view in the matter. I am glad now to be able to do so.
In the first place, as the hon. member who has just spoken has indicated, we must be clear in our own minds as to the basis of our original intervention in Korea. It was not for the purpose of supporting or removing any Korean government, whether that government was bad or whether it was good; rather it was to defeat aggression and to carry out our obligations as a member of the United Nations.
Although that has been the purpose of United Nations intervention, as a country participating in this collective operation we cannot refrain from indicating our interest in what goes on in Korea itself. We certainly have an interest in such developments, and for at least three reasons. In the first place, the political objective of the United Nations in Korea-and that, of course, is to be contrasted with the military objective-as stated in the United Nations resolutions is to establish in that country a free, united and democratic government.
Secondly, any division and disturbance, to say nothing of civil outbreaks behind the lines, endangers the military position. We must always keep that in mind. It would be an ironic tragedy indeed if United Nations forces in Korea, there to keep the aggressor out, should have to be used to keep the peace among those people whom we are attempting to assist.
Thirdly, we have an interest because, as a member of the United Nations, we are participating in the relief and rehabilitation of Korea itself. So these events, though they may seem to be domestic in a certain sense, are events which must arouse our interest and concern. And they have done that, as is already indicated by the questions asked in the house.
I think it is no exaggeration to say that these developments in South Korea have been unhappy and, in a sense, dangerous to the
3484	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs accomplishment of the United Nations objective there. The situation is not good from that point of view, and it does not seem to be improving-though constructive efforts are being made by United Nations agencies and by other governments to bring about a solution.
The present situation really dates from May 28 when martial law was declared in Pusan and in the area surrounding Pusan, and when certain members of the national assembly were arrested. We made inquiries about these events and, having satisfied ourselves as to what had actually happened, we addressed a communication to the Secretary General of the United Nations. For his part the Secretary General expressed his concern to the United Nations commission for the unification and rehabilitation of Korea in the following words:
I have been following with deep anxiety the difficulties that exist between the executive and legislative branches of the government of the Republic of Korea and I have constantly and strongly endorsed the efforts of the United Nations commission to co-operate with the government in ensuring conditions of political stability within the country.
Strict adherence to constitutional and democratic processes are all the more necessary in a country which must nurse and develop all of its resources to join members of the United Nations in repelling aggression and in promoting economic recovery. It is, of course, the responsibility of the Korean people and representatives to choose their own public servants but the United Nations, and especially those members providing assistance in Korea, cannot remain unconcerned when arbitrary methods are used which threaten to destroy the roots of democratic government. From the beginning of the United Nations responsibilities in Korea, there has been a paramount concern, expressed in every discussion on Korea in United Nations organs, that conditions should be created which would encourage the steady development of democratic, constitutional government.
And then he concluded his message by saying:
You-
That is, the United Nations commission for the unification and rehabilitation of Korea.
-have my continuing support in your efforts to assist the government in bringing the crisis to an end and in bringing the blessings of good government to the Korean people.
I should be grateful to have you bring this message to the attention of the president of the republic.
I understand that that was done. We also hoped that the United Nations commission might be successful in its intervention to settle the dispute between President Rhee and his assembly. Syngman Rhee, the head of the Korean government, is a great Korean patriot and indeed has been considered by his people, and I suppose rightly so, as the architect of their freedom. He commands great support in that country and he remains its outstanding personality. Indeed our


information is that there is no other comparable personality around which a strong government could rally. Therefore, it would be tragic if the end of the career of this great Korean patriot should be signalized by the destruction of democratic freedom and the rule of law in Korea.
We feel, and other governments which have expressed their concern feel, that if the Korean constitution has to be changed it should be done by lawful process and not by what has been termed, I believe, in the article which my hon. friend just read, a one-man revolution. I am sure that all hon. members will join me in hoping that the president of the Korean republic, who we all realize has held office in a period of great difficulty and cruel suffering by his people, will heed the friendly counsel that has been given and permit the normal processes of democratic government to be upheld in that country at a time when the menace from the north remains so great.
Neither Korea nor the United Nations can afford to have political disturbances behind the lines nor to permit the purpose of the United Nations or the safety of United Nations soldiers to be prejudiced by political intrigue and ambition.

Mr. Chairman, because of the sort of literature that has been coming to us and the press reports which have been published condemning the minister of external affairs, I think someone should stand up in this house and say that we are backing him to the limit in his work and plans for the peace of the world. It may be my nature to be impatient with these peace propagandists, but I think they should get after Russia because of the recent attacks made on Sweden and other places.
If the dominion government through the minister of external affairs had not supported the United States in stopping aggression in Korea, where would Korea be today? Where would Sweden be? Where would Norway be? Where would Finland be? Where would Denmark be? Where would we be later on? I know that the great Peacemaker says, blessed are the peacemakers, but He also said:
Neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
I have admired the outstanding patience of the minister and I hope he will just carry on cheerfully and thoroughly and be one of those ready to say to those who deserve it: So far shall you come and no further.

I urge the minister to guard with utmost exactitude the sovereignty of Canada in all of his external contacts and relations.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take up with the minister a question which has been raised before concerning the safety of Canadians in China. This question in the main has revolved around the fate of Canadian missionaries in China. I want to make it perfectly clear that although my remarks will relate to the fate of Canadian missionaries, I am not concerned exclusively with
Supply-External Affairs missionaries or those of any one religious denomination, but with the fate of the comparatively large number-I use the words "large number" under the circumstances-of Canadians still in China.
I do not think it is necessary to rehearse at this time the discussion I had previously which was based on the statement made by the Prime Minister on April 21 as to the situation of some Canadian missionaries and sisters in Chinese prisons. On the basis of that statement it was suggested that the Prime Minister was minimizing the dangers and hardships they were undergoing. I have had correspondence with the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs on that point, and it certainly appears that every effort is being made, within the limits of current policy, first to find out exactly what the situation is, and then to do what can be done, again within the limits of current policy, to make certain that the treatment of Canadians is mitigated so far as possible. My remarks now are directed rather toward the limits of current policy.
The minister has consistently stated in discussing these matters that, because of the unpredictable nature of the communist regime in China, because it is not prone to have regard to what other governments say about it and to follow their advice, it has been his feeling and the feeling of his department that to criticize or make strong statements with respect to the treatment accorded to Canadians in China would probably do more harm than good and would prejudice the safety of Canadian nationals rather than improve their position. I think there is room for controversy regarding that policy quite apart from the question whether or not we have done all we can to look after our people over there. It is suggested that the policy of soft words and of extreme caution in discussing these matters which has been followed by the minister has, instead of assisting Canadian nationals in China, made their position worse because it has been taken by the communist government as an indication of weakness or lack of interest.
I know that you cannot make predictions as to how this peculiar form of ideology will react in the people who profess it. We cannot tell how they are going to react to anything we may say, but it certainly comes to mind that the communists believe in displays of toughness. They follow that policy themselves and I think we have seen through the communists' own methods in other situations that the only thing which the communists respect is strength. While I know we are not in a position to intervene actively in China, nevertheless it does occur to me that we might apply the same policy to our

Supply-External Affairs expressions of concern and our intentions with respect to looking after the welfare of our nationals in China. In this regard I was interested in an article appearing on page 3 of the May 31st issue of The Ensign. It is a dispatch from Hong Kong and reads as follows:
A clear call to the press of the west to "tell the world" of the bitter and cruel persecution of the Christian church and its missionaires in China has been issued here by the editorial board of the China Missionary Bulletin.
I am sorry that I have to confess that I am not absolutely certain of my facts but I believe that the China Missionary Bulletin is not a Catholic organ although it is referred to in The Ensign which is a Catholic paper. I believe I can say that it carries additional weight in the sense that it represents several denominations. The article continues:
"Conditions for the church and for humanity in China are so bad that the world must be told about them," the board declares. Although there must be "due regard for the well-being of the heroic bishops, priests and people there," nonetheless, "the sad and painful" story must be told. "Suppression of clearly confirmed news will not serve to lighten the burden of the priests and people there," the board writes. "But it will play into the very hands of the communist terrorists who consistently use fear as a trump card. This must be understood: the free world can no longer afford to be duped by the Red game. The tendency to hold back news for fear of reprisals must be re-examined and reevaluated," the board says pointing out that "Catholic missioners generally have not been prone to science. The differences between the world visions of communism and Christianity are so irreconcilable and the stakes are so high that there can be no minimizing of the horrors of communist terror. Remaining silent more often than not means falling victim to the communist game."
In the same issue on the same page there is also a report of an interview with two nuns who were imprisoned in China in which they themselves say that it is necessary and desirable that there should be the maximum publicity given to the maltreatment accorded to Canadian missionaries by the communist authorities in China. When you have the missionaries themselves, who it seems to me are the ones who know the conditions and who are the ones who would suffer if the policy should be wrong, saying that a policy of giving maximum publicity is not wrong, then I think we must consider very carefully whether we are following the right course in using cautious expressions and the gentle word, which has been the policy followed by the minister to date.
I do not want to do the minister an injustice and confuse two things. I believe that there must be caution in that what we say is based on fact. We must not make statements as to numbers or conditions when we do not know that those statements are absolutely accurate. However, I believe that

once the fact is established-and there have been several facts established with respect to persecution and ill treatment-then I believe the strongest of language and the strongest of condemnation is called for. It is that policy that I would ask the minister to review and to say whether he does not feel that the time has now arrived for the strongest possible condemnation of the maltreatment which these Canadians have been receiving in China, not just because they are missionaries but because they are Canadian nationals and are engaged in works of charity and mercy.

speechtext: Before the minister replies, I should like to draw his attention to one feature of the same subject. What co-operation exists between the Canadian government and the United States government which is also interested and which is responsible for many United States nationals who are in that country? During the past week I had a letter from the Passionist organization. Bishop O'Gara of Ottawa is the head of that organization in China. Together with five other Passionist fathers he has been under house arrest for the last two years. When the minister is replying will he tell us what the existing policy is with regard to co-operation with the United States in this respect?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity to make a statement on this important matter, and I might deal first with the points that have been made last. I would say that we have maintained close co-operation with the United States in respect of the nationals of both our countries who are in China. We exchange information and views as to what can most effectively be done. We are both in the same position in the sense that neither government has any representation in China. As I recall, the last intervention that was made was made on behalf of the United States and Canada by the United Kingdom representative in Peking.
In so far as the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops are concerned, I do not admit that we have indulged in soft words as the best means of assisting Canadians in China. If the hon. gentleman will read some of the statements that have been made in the house I think he will find some words which could hardly be considered as soft because the treatment that has been meted out to certain Canadians in China and to other westerners would not deserve soft words in describing it. It has been brutal treatment. It is bad enough, however, without exaggerating it, and that brutal treatment has not been applied to all Canadians..

It has been suggested outside the house in journalistic quarters that we have intervened too weakly and, I believe, that we have only intervened recently. The fact is we have intervened a good many times through the channels which are open to us. We have intervened in more than one way, not merely through the United Kingdom representative in Peking, though I am not in a position for obvious reasons to make public all the machinery that we have used in this matter. It has been suggested that we should have been stronger in our intervention and stronger in our denunciations and protests. The hon. member for Kamloops has indicated that communists are only impressed by a display of force. I agree with that, but I should add that my experience is that they have never been very much impressed by displays of verbal force alone. They carefully examine the material force which is behind the words you use. If you have not got ways and means of carrying out your statements, then they will not be impressed by them.

speechtext:
In the interventions and statements we have made, we have acted on the best advice we could obtain from our own experts and from other governments which were helping us, as to the manner of protest most effectively designed to help those we were trying to help. In the notes that we have sent, and in the statements we have made, the language we have used has been at least as strong as that used by other governments in the representations they have made.
In the letter which I wrote the hon. member for Kamloops dated May 9, and which I think has been made public, I concluded with the following words:
You will agree, I am sure, that our primary concern in this matter must be for the safety and wellbeing of the more than one hundred Canadians still in China. From the outset of the troubles in that country, this has, in my opinion, made it desirable to keep statements upon as realistic and factual a basis as possible. These unfortunate people are exposed in a position where no one can help them if the communist authorities choose to ill-treat them. Therefore the utmost circumspection in public discussion is obviously desirable, and more restraint has to be shown than our feelings in the matter would dictate.
In this same letter to the hon. member I attempted to remove any impression that the Prime Minister's earlier statement might have left that we were a little cool to some
Supply-External Affairs of the mistreatment to which Canadians had been subjected. I included the following words:
It is not easy to measure degrees of maltreatment. When the Prime Minister used the words "Canadians had not in general been physically maltreated," he was thinking of torture or anything causing bodily harm or permanent disability and he gave, I think, an accurate picture of the situation of the great majority of Canadians in China. However, I am well aware that the three Sisters of the Immaculate Conception who reached Hong Kong two months ago were subjected, if not to physical maltreatment, to the most degrading ordeals during and after their "trial." They were paraded through the streets where the mob was encouraged to spit upon them and to pelt them with filth. Others have suffered similar experiences. We understand that they have borne up well despite the hardships they have undergone, and it is thought, certainly it is hoped, that they will suffer no serious aftereffects.
For obvious reasons, Mr. Chairman, we can never be absolutely certain of our information, but the factual situation in regard to the number of Canadians remaining in China seems to be as follows: On March 12, there were 168 Canadians still in China. On June 9, there were 121, so during the previous three months some had been able to get out. Of those 121, 40 are Catholic nuns; 39 are Catholic priests; 6 are Protestant missionaries with 1 dependent; 6 are non-Asiatic Canadians and 29 are Chinese Canadians. It is reported that of this number still in China, 7 are in prison, 4 sisters and 3 priests; 15 are under house arrest, 3 sisters and 12 priests. During the last few months 9 Canadians who had been in prison have arrived at Hong Kong, 3 sisters, 2 Protestant missionaries and 4 priests.

This report is by Dr. Kilborn, a medical missionary, and it has been circulated within the last few days by the board of overseas missions of the United Church of

Supply-External Affairs Canada. I have read no more impressive report of conditions in China, and no more damning indictment of the reason for the deterioration of those conditions and of the attitude of the Chinese communists towards westerners.

speechtext:
We have had several answers which have explained the position of the government in regard to specific points, Mr. Chairman, which have been raised this morning. But it is in regard to the wider implications of this discussion that I should like to address my remarks. At the very outset I wish to suggest that we ought to ask ourselves what it is we really are discussing on this lovely June morning. What is it that is before the house at this time?
This is the first item in the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. It is the first opportunity that has been presented for several weeks-in fact, one might say two or three months-for a general discussion of external affairs. For that reason I believe we should ask ourselves exactly what it is that is before us. We are discussing survival. We are discussing our survival as a free nation, and the survival of western civilization; that is what we are discussing. Yet, we have an atmosphere of almost complete unreality in dealing with survival itself.
It is true that the first item of the estimates deals with the financial problems of the department, but it is the basis of a general debate. Events have occurred that have profoundly affected the position of this country and of the free world. The attention of the minister was drawn to something that he has done. It was pointed out that in the opinion of one hon. member it had not been wise to seize on this opportunity to publicly announce criticism of the course followed by the United States army in its direction of military affairs in Korea. I do not think the opening words of the reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs should be passed over without comment. In reply to something which certainly should have been raised in this chamber, because it is something that has been commented upon generally in the press throughout Canada, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in commenting upon the statement made by the hon. member for Broadview, said, "I am grateful to him for his advice on diplomacy." No hon. member sitting in this committee was unaware of the sarcasm behind that remark. That sarcasm was recognized by the laughter on the other side of the chamber which greeted his statement.
I wish to refer to that comment for this reason. Any attempt that has been made by the members of this party to present a unified

front in principle on every possible occasion, so that no comfort could be taken by Russia or any other possible enemy in any evidence of disunity with regard to matters of basic principle, should not, I hope, be taken by the government as an admission that we are to be treated like children and are to be admonished any time we point out to the government things that we think should be corrected.
After all, truth is largely the result of open and free controversy. The very purpose of freedom of speech and freedom of exchange of ideas by every means of communication now open to us is not merely that people may have the pleasure of speech but that truth may result from the exchange of discussion and the exchange of ideas which take place in that way. When it comes to questions of principle, we want to be sure that, wherever it is possible, there be unity and agreement without regard to party affiliation so that it may be known that Canada stands united in every effective step that may be taken for the defence of freedom and of our civilization.
But we must examine what it was that the minister regarded as something which it was almost an affront to mention. The handling of a single infantry company was the occasion for headlines in relation to something that could easily have been dealt with by a private exchange of correspondence or by a telephone call. Whether the intention was what has been suggested by some editorials or whether it was not, the fact remains that this protest was regarded by responsible publications in the United States as something which was hardly in keeping with the relationship between Canada and the United States.
It should not at any time be suggested that we take our directions from comments in the United States. Nevertheless, at a time when we are seeking to strengthen the great partnership of the free nations of the western world, we must not ignore the effect of statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, by the Prime Minister or by any other member of the government which speaks for the whole of Canada in international affairs. For that reason I would point out that this is not a case of someone presuming to come into this chamber and advise the minister on diplomacy. Even though the minister may not think that it is for him to take advice of that kind, I would point out that others have expressed their comments on this matter. For instance, a responsible publication in the capital of the United States, namely the Washington Post, referred to the note so much publicized by the

Secretary of State for External Affairs as a silly note. It went further; and I quote from what was said in an editorial in the Washington Post in relation to this statement:
Actually the Canadian protest to the United States about dispatch of Canadian troops to Koje without prior approval from Ottawa was more than a trifle silly.
The request reportedly was cleared with the British commonwealth commander in Korea who seemingly neglected to inform Ottawa. It would be ridiculous, of course, if a field commander had to seek government approval for every tactical disposition of troops. Either Canadian troops are part of a U.N. army or they are not. If they are. then the principle of international command must apply just as it applies to other troops in Korea.
That is the end of the quotation that I propose to read from that editorial. I mention this editorial which expressed sentiments similar to those which appeared elsewhere in the United States. I think that we as a nation must be extremely careful, and that the government which expresses the voice of Canada on behalf of all of us in international affairs must be extremely careful-and I think it is our duty to say that they must be careful-when they are dealing with something in relation to military activity in an area in which such an overwhelming preponderance of the responsibility for success rests in the hands of the government of the United States and the military commanders of the United States.
We are proud-and justifiably so-of the manner in which young Canadians have on this occasion carried forward the great traditions of this country, as they have done whenever we have been called upon as a people to assume our military responsibilities. The fact remains, however, that the overwhelming burden is being borne by the people of the United States. We must be extremely careful that we do not suggest to them that we are unconscious of the burden they are carrying or the sacrifices they are making. I also think that we should be extremely careful that we do not at any time say things which would in any way interfere with this great friendship of ours.
The only reason that I have raised this matter at this time is that when this point was raised this morning, the Secretary of State for External Affairs brushed it off as though it was almost an affront that it was raised here. I suggest that the House of Commons and the people of Canada who are behind Canadian efforts to build up the combined strength of the nations of the western world would have welcomed some indication by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he himself thought the protest was a little bit silly and that we are not going to see any repetition of incidents of that kind.
Supply-External Affairs
We are now coming to the close of another session, and what is happening at this time is just exactly what we predicted would happen toward the close of this session. It will be recalled that at the very beginning of this session, on a number of occasions, we urged that the government place before the house the business with which we would be called upon to deal in a manner that would give us a continuing sense of reality, the opportunity for early debate and for the presentation of arguments which not only could impress themselves upon the members of the house but also convey to the people of Canada-through the press, the radio and otherwise-information with regard to the subjects which were before those who have been sent here as their elected representatives to do the business of Canada. At the time those suggestions were made, they were treated with scorn by the government. In fact, the attitude taken was that we were being rather presumptuous in telling the government what it should do about the business of the house.
Here we find ourselves with several important committees still meeting, which draw members from this chamber. We find ourselves with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence still to be dealt with, as well as other important departments. All this has helped to create the atmosphere of unreality in which this present debate is now projected. It has been the result either of planned frustration or of complete failure by the government to understand how the business of this house can be carried forward in an orderly and efficient manner. It is one or the other. Hon. members are left to guess until the last minutes of the session at night what they are going to deal with the following day. Debates cannot be planned. Important measures are brought forward at the last moment.

speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the leader of the opposition. speechtext:
I was pointing out the reason for the atmosphere of unreality which must be apparent to every member who is sitting in this house, and I said all that I propose to say in regard to the incompetence and the planned frustration which have resulted in this situation.

Supply-External Affairs
Today we have reason for hope, and great reason for hope, that the growing strength of the western allies is going to fulfil the hopes and dreams of those who have supported the principles that have been put forward on behalf of Canada by this government. But there is no reason to treat this situation lightly. Too often subjects of the most far-reaching consequence have been dealt with in a casual manner, which has helped to convey to the people of Canada the impression that there is not that measure of urgency which I believe should be in the mind of every Canadian at this time. I would recall merely as an example, that when a situation arose in Berlin a short time ago which easily could have provided the spark that would have ignited all the combustible material that has been built up in that area, the Secretary of State for External Affairs summed up the situation in these words:
There will undoubtedly be fireworks, but there is no reason for panic over the giant crackers or for relief over the rockets that burst in the form of a dove.
Words of that kind may possibly be useful on occasion. Apt expressions often are more useful than extended arguments in illustrating a point. I do suggest, however, that the gravity of the present situation is such that on every occasion when the events of the moment are described by the Secretary of State for External Affairs he should use words which will leave no doubt in the minds of the public that these are not fireworks, but that we are confronted with the most critical situation that has ever confronted free nations except in time of general war.
It is even possible that never before have we been confronted with as critical a situation as today, because if we lose this struggle we lose freedom not only for years but for generations.
So that we may get this subject in its proper perspective I should like to quote from a book which has just been published by Drew Middleton, the head of the New York Times European bureau, under the title "Defence of Western Europe". I do so because he is generally regarded as one of the most competent observers of international affairs. He has written this book as a result of interviews with officers and civilians who have escaped from behind the iron curtain. He has written it as a result of confidential discussion with men of the highest authority. For that very reason it is one of the very significant books of this year, and perhaps of many years. I should like to quote from this very recent and very important book, pointing out that we are now in the most vital period of this cold war, which can become a hot war at any time.


He points out that we are at the same stage in relation to Russian preparation that we were in relation to German preparation two years before the outbreak of the last war. He points out that the production of Soviet Russia and its satellites is rapidly mounting to a crescendo, and that within two years it will have reached its peak. For that very reason, if Russia contemplates war, 1954 is the target year for any efforts that we should be making.
He does not approach this subject with the thought that war is inevitable. On the contrary, what he is trying to do with all the vigour, with all the earnestness and with all the sense of reality of one of the really great war correspondents and military observers of modern times, is to point out to the people of the free world, while there is yet time, that we are not going to coast by any easy route into the distant lands of promised peace; but that if we are going to have the kind of peace that we want we are going to pay for it in effort and in money.
What he seeks to point out by the most earnest argument is that we must put forward every effort with a sense of the utmost urgency; that there can be no easy course, and that we are certainly going to feel the strain of our effort if that effort is to be successful. In a nutshell, what he tells us is to remember that those who have examined the records tell us today that if only the free world had displayed such unity in 1939 they could have prevented the war even with all the German preparations. The question is whether, with that evidence so recently before our eyes, we are going to prevent another war, when preparations on an immensely greater scale are taking place within exactly the same pattern today.
Then he refers to the statements of General Mast, the great French general. We may well listen to what he says about General Mast's observations, just as we might wish today that we had listened to the advice of General de Gaulle in the days before the last world war. The French army's collapse in 1940 was certainly not the fault of that officer of great foresight and great vision who predicted the manner in which any armoured threat might be met and might be overcome. He made his predictions in words that unfortunately were picked up and copied by General Guderian and other German armoured commanders for the purpose of organizing their forces in a manner that brought such dramatic and terrible success. I refer to that because perhaps the very fact that General Mast is no longer an active member of the French general staff may incline some to forget the importance that is attached by many people to the views that he has put forward. I quote now

from Drew Middleton's book, and shall continue to quote until I indicate that the quotation is ended:
The first point made by General Mast is that although our present concepts of Soviet power are based on the peacetime strength of the Russian military, naval and air services, we should be confronted, after a partial mobilization, with 250 divisions of ground troops, 20,000-30,000 aircraft and more than 300 submarines. After three months of full mobilization there would be 350 divisions; this figure would rise to 500 divisions by the end of the first year of war.
This is the basis, General Mast points out, on which the West must make its calculations if it wishes to avoid, in an infinitely more important arena, the underestimates made at the beginning of the Korean war.
I am still quoting from Drew Middleton's book where he refers to General Mast's book:
Although this book is concerned principally with Europe and its defences, it is worth quoting General Mast's appreciation of the direction of the Soviet attacks in time of war. He lists them as:
1.	A naval, air and ground attack in the Arctic aimed at the capture of Alaska and Iceland.
2.	An air-ground attack in the Middle East aimed at the occupation of Persia, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the isthmus of Suez.
3.	An air-ground attack on western Europe and North Africa aimed at the conquest of all Europe and the elimination of western military power from the entire North African shore of the Mediterranean.
4.	A harassing action in East Asia (Korea and Japan) accompanied by indirect action, carried out by China, in southeast Asia.
5.	World-wide naval action by submarines against the seaborne transport of the anti-Soviet coalition.
It is General Mast's contention that the Soviet union will be capable of undertaking all these operations simultaneously. He divides the forces allotted to these operations as follows:
Alaska and Iceland, 3 to 6 divisions and 1,500 aircraft;
The Middle East, 40 to 60 divisions and 5,000 aircraft;
The Far East, 20 Soviet divisions and 5,000 aircraft, plus Chinese reinforcements.
For the European theatre of operations, General Mast divides the effort in this way:
Scandinavia, 15 to 17 divisions and 1,000 aircraft;
Western Europe, 120 divisions, initially, gradually increased to 180-190 divisions plus 10,000 aircraft;
The Balkans, 35 divisions plus 1,500 aircraft plus the armies of the satellite states. These latter we will discuss in detail later.
Thus a general officer of the highest professional qualifications. The numbers seem like figures in a nightmare, rising and falling before one's eyes. Yet they represent the capacity of the great power complex with which we are now faced.
That is the end of the quotation from Drew Middleton's book that I propose to put on the record. These are Drew Middleton's words: "The numbers seem like figures in a nightmare, rising and falling before one's eyes". Yes, they are a nightmare. Those in this chamber who saw the effect of military superiority when it was directed by the German general staff from 1914 to 1918 and again from 1939 to 1945 know what military superiority at the outset of any war really means. They know the terror; they know the
Supply-External Affairs anguish; they know the horror of trying to build defence forces under pressure of that kind, of trying to meet the threat of superiority of that nature, which constantly approaches nearer to complete and utter victory.
Right across this country today there is a challenge to those who have seen what that kind of thing means, a challenge to create in the minds of our people-and there is a similar challenge in other free nations to create in the minds of their people-a sense of urgency and a sense of reality in the face of nightmare figures of that kind.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, and with such truth, that Russia is never very much impressed by verbal force. He told us just a short time ago that they examine what real force lies behind the statements that are made. I am suggesting that the statements that are made here at this time, statements that are made with that nightmare reality before us and with other balancing considerations before us, must be assessed with a full recognition of what it is we are trying to do, and the purpose towards which the combined efforts of the free nations are directed, both in the Atlantic and the Pacific areas at the present time.
One hon. member said a short time ago that we should say to Russia, "Thus far shalt thou go, and no farther." By all means, let us say that. But with what? If the Secretary of State for External Affairs is correct in his analysis of the Russian position, then, unless we are resting entirely upon our confidence in the atomic bomb, let us assess quite carefully what it is we are hoping to do to meet figures of the kind I have just put forward.
What I wish to emphasize particularly is that the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence do go hand in hand in preparing for the defence of freedom of the Canadian people at this time. It is the function of the Department of External Affairs to make the international arrangements and to assist in creating the pattern within which our military contribution forms part of the great international framework devoted to the hope of peace and security.
We all recognize that with a population of 14 million people, as compared with the 160 million in the United States, the more than 50 million in Great Britain, the nearly 50 million in France, the more than 50 million in Italy, and all the other millions in the other free nations of western Europe, we are of course only a part, and perhaps a relatively small part, in that great team which is now building its strength for the defence of

Supply-External Affairs ail the free nations which are confronted with the threat represented by the figures I have just placed on record.
We certainly will support what is done in that respect. But to give reality to the enormous sums which will soon be asked from this House of Commons for purposes of national defence, it is important that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in a much clearer manner than has yet been done, should put before the house exactly the pattern into which this military contribution is going to fit.
On earlier occasions members of this party have put forward the contention that we should be re-examining our military organizations, that we should be remembering that military logistics suggest that our effort should be directed to the building up of the most compact, hard-hitting and mobile forces in view of the fact that, of necessity, in any combined effort, they will likely be moved far from the shores of Canada to keep any threat away from us.
The possibility of having a discussion in regard to that subject in terms of complete reality would suggest the advisability of our knowing much more than we now know of what was really discussed at Lisbon, what was discussed earlier here in Ottawa and what was discussed elsewhere, so that we may not simply have the bland assurance that what we are doing meets with the approval of the NATO organization. Rather we want to know what the real plan is and be ready to support it and contribute our part to that plan consistent with the best possible use of the industrial and other opportunities that we do possess.
In saying this I wish to place before the committee at this time the suggestion that we remember the vital importance of Europe to Canada, to the United States and to the free world, not merely as the home from which our civilization sprang but rather as to what it means today in the contribution it could make to the combined strength of the free world. It is not just the great historic territory west of the iron curtain; it is not just the area in which our culture found its expression before it came to this continent; it is not just the area where 200 million vigorous, educated and cultured people live and are bound to live in the future.
Let us think of what it means to the balance of military power if under any circumstances, either by military aggression or by political action, western Europe, the cradle of our civilization, came under the domination of the Kremlin. Think of what it would mean in terms of the great gun plants, of the great armament factories, of


the aircraft factories and of the naval bases. Think of what it would mean if all that production were under integrated control. Think of what it would mean if throughout the whole of Europe, from which modern industry emerged, they were pouring out guns, tanks, aircrafts, machines of war as well as ships and the other military requirements of world power.
Let us remember, simply as an example, what the occupation of Poland, of Czechoslovakia, and of East Germany has meant to Russia where they have been able to take over the Bergenhutton steel plant of Poland, the Skoda plant at Pilsen and the great gun and armament plants of East Germany. The reason our troops and the troops of the United Nations are undergoing such difficulties in Korea today, the main reason perhaps why the communists may well be planning the delays that are now taking place, is that the highly developed industrial and military skill of East Germany, Czechoslovakia and southern Poland are now under the most dreadful compulsion to work for the Soviet empire.
Think of what it would mean if all the great gun plants of the whole of Germany, of France, of Italy, of Belgium, of Holland, yes and of Britain as well, were under unified control. Think of what it would mean if all those plants were producing aircraft to a single design. Think of what it would mean if they were producing submarine parts in all countries of Europe to be assembled at the naval bases in the Baltic, on the Atlantic coast and in the Mediterranean.
This is not a distant possibility; this is an immediate possibility unless the plans we are making bear fruit and preserve us from the threat that is constantly before our eyes. The Schuman plan for the unification of steel production in Europe has not yet reached fulfilment but it would become a dreadful reality under the most terrifying form of integration. Think of what that would achieve under the awful compulsion by which they would employ the brains to direct those operations.
I have reviewed these possibilities simply to suggest that we get back to reality. We are not discussing ordinary administrative problems of government, we are discussing nothing less than the survival of our civilization. Canada will never stand alone. Canada has indicated, and the government has expressed, that opinion with the full and unqualified support of the members of this house. But there has been plenty of evidence that the people of Canada have not found in the statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs or in the interpretation

of our position by this government that sense of urgency and reality which conveys to their minds the necessity for the amount of cooperation which will prevent a third world war.
Whatever differences of opinion there may have been, and some of those differences have been expressed in recent days, whatever may have been said this morning about our desire for a more dignified and more co-operative point of view on Canada's part which recognizes our place on this great team of free nations, it is with our eyes on the future and the understanding of all that another world war would mean that I urge with all the sense of urgency I can express that we keep in mind what Canada has suffered already in two world wars and realize how much more terrible a third world war would be.
I am simply urging that in our discussion of the affairs of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence we keep before our eyes at all times the fact that nothing less than the most effective use of the great strength of the free nations will prevent another world war and keep that peace which is our one and only purpose.
There are many people in Canada today whose relatives live beyond the iron curtain. They ask themselves what hope there is of being reunited eventually, within their own lives, with those they left in the lands where they were born.
Today in this country people of German stock whose relatives are now in Eastern Germany, people of Polish stock, of Hungarian, Bulgarian, Roumanian, Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian, Ukrainian and Chinese stocks, yes, of Russian stock as well, are all asking whether the present division of this old world of ours is permanent or whether the efforts that we are making to prevent war and preserve peace is something that offers some hope, in the years ahead, of their being able to rejoin their relatives, meet them again and establish those contacts that decent human beings all wish to maintain. In the plans that we are making today I think we should offer hope not only that these plans contemplate a static peace but also that in due course the strength of our position may offer the opportunity to all nations to determine their own form of government and the way they will live as they were promised in the charter of the United Nations when it was signed in San Francisco in the spring of 1945.
This surely is a hope that will give new spirit, encouragement and faith to many people today who are constantly suffering the anguish of complete separation from those who are so dear to them. In that regard I
Supply-External Affairs think we should remember that for long years in the past there have been great associations of nations which maintained peace by the strength of their defences. Then in the course of years there were improvements in the relations between those nations, and ultimately they came closer and closer together. In the early days of the present century we came very close to establishing the kind of world in which there would be a constant freedom of movement, in which people could not only exchange ideas but also move freely from land to land. It is difficult for us to realize today that in the early days of the present century it was possible for a person to move around this world of ours without a passport, and that it was even possible for people to move with almost complete freedom in Russia itself when they visited that country.
That is a kind of world we have almost forgotten but that was a kind of world which emerged, with all its weaknesses and all its faults, at a time when the combined strength of free nations preserved peace against the threat of aggression. I would hope that we may not only look to a static peace in which there will be great armed camps on one side of the iron curtain and great armed camps on the other side but that we may also look forward to the day, distant though it may be, when in God's good time the fortitude, understanding of their purpose and the combined strength of the free nations will not only offer the hope of peace and security to us but will bring to those nations now in slavery the promised peace and freedom which they were assured by the charter of the United Nations.
It is with that dream, it is with that hope of a day when even the people of Russia may find that freedom which they have so richly earned by their own sacrifices in time of war, that I urge that we cast our eyes toward the very real world in which we live at this time, and that we discuss all these problems in terms of cold reality. At times when one hears some of the exchanges that take place, when one hears explanations that seem to have so little regard for the fantastic figures of the military might to which we are opposed, it almost seems as though the one thing that would do any good would be for all men to go out and shout at the top of their lungs, through megaphones amplified by every loud speaking device that would give their voices strength: "For the love of all that is dear and sacred to the people of Canada today, wake up!"

Mr. Chairman, I think at least the earlier remarks of the hon. gentleman deserve some comment from me, and

Supply-External Affairs for the next minute or two I propose to make that comment. I suggest to the hon. gentleman that when he mentioned my opening words he should also have mentioned the opening words of the hon. member who preceded me and who in those words stated that this action of the Canadian government in defence of a principle to which it is committed, and to which I think the Canadian people are committed, was inspired by a publicity machine. If those remarks had not been made by the hon. member for Broadview, possibly my opening remarks might not have been made in the same tone as they were. That, I think, sufficiently explains the way this subject was introduced by me.
The leader of the opposition indicated that we on this side will not accept either advice or criticism on such an important matter as foreign affairs. I assure him-and I do not need to assure the committee-that the government on this particular subject, as on other subjects, is always very glad indeed to accept criticism and advice. We have no illusions of either omniscience or infallibility. The Koje matter arose-and I do not wish to labour the point-because of a principle to which we attach importance, and we declared our support of that principle and our understanding of its importance by a statement in the house. The hon. gentleman has stated, and I have no quarrel with him in the statement, that it has caused a great deal of attention, especially in the United States. He has read from an estimable and highly regarded United States newspaper, the Washington Post, which described our intervention on this occasion as a silly note. I submit that the Washington Post rather misunderstood the Canadian position, but if the hon. gentleman wishes to associate himself with that description of our intervention to protect the entity of the Canadian brigade in circumstances which were not governed by military considerations I have no quarrel with him.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I should like to refer back briefly, Mr. Chairman, to a discussion we had this morning on the Koje incident. I am trying to satisfy myself about this question of the timing of the protest which was sent to the United States government. In a moment I shall ask the minister to answer one or two questions.
On May 26 the minister made a statement in the house, as recorded at page 2552 of Hansard for that day. He said:
The government feels that it is essential that the Canadian policy in respect of the breaking up of the Canadian brigade for miscellaneous duties in Korea should be made clear. A note has accordingly been presented to the state department in Washington.
From that, one would assume that a formal diplomatic note had been sent off by the time the minister spoke in the house at three o'clock in the afternoon. However, two days later there is a United Press dispatch from Washington which reads as follows:
The state department said today that it sympathizes with Canada's objections to the assignment of Canadian troops to the Koje island prison camp. However, department spokesman Mr. Michael J. McDermott said that it has not given Canada any formal assurances pending the arrival of a formal diplomatic note.
On the afternoon of May 28, as recorded at page 2659 of Hansard for that day, the hon. member for Peel asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs the following question:
May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether or not he has found out what has caused the delay in the mails between Ottawa and Washington with respect to some of his recent correspondence with the United States government?
The minister replied as follows:
As far as I know there has been no delay whatever in this matter. I assume the hon. member is referring to the statement which I made on Monday. That statement was in the hands of the United States state department in Washington, and indeed in the hands of the United States embassy in Ottawa, before it was given to the house.

You will notice that the minister mentions a "statement" but not a note. Later on that same day we had another United Press dispatch from Washington which was filed at ten o'clock at night and which says:
Canada sent a formal note to the United States today, demanding that it be consulted on any future decisions to split up units of Canadian forces serving in Korea.
As I understand it, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, there is a difference between a formal diplomatic note and a statement. As I understand it, a statement is a sort of memorandum, sent between one government and another, and which requires no answer. A formal diplomatic note is a formal message between two governments that requires an answer.
From the news dispatches I have read, and the statements in the house, I am led to believe that, although the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a statement to the house on Monday, May 26, a formal diplomatic note was not received by the state department in Washington until forty-eight hours later. Perhaps a statement might have been received, but not the formal diplomatic note which was required. Can the minister clarify that situation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Yes, I think I can clear up the point that is troubling the hon. member. The timing of those events to which he has referred is as follows: Before the statement which I gave to the house upon the Koje matter was made on May 26 our ambassador in Washington had left a copy of that statement with the state department. In diplomatic parlance, I suppose it would have been called an oral note-a note of the statement that I was to make that afternoon in the House of Commons in Ottawa. A copy of that statement was handed also to a representative of the United States embassy in Ottawa. It is, therefore, strictly accurate to say-no matter what press reports may have stated to the contrary-that the statement which was made in the House of Commons in Ottawa was made after its contents had been conveyed to the United States government through the state department and through the United States embassy in Ottawa.
When the state department received this oral note from the ambassador they said that if a formal reply were desired it would be preferable to resubmit the oral note in the form of a formal diplomatic note. That was done the next day, and a formal reply was received the day before yesterday. The actual terms of the statement, in the form of an oral note delivered by the ambassador to the state department and by this department to the United States embassy here, were in the
Supply-External Affairs possession of the United States government before the statement was made.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
