speechtext: Would it not have been desirable to send off a diplomatic note at the same time as the statement was made in this house, especially in dealing with a touchy matter such as this? Does the minister not consider that might have been a desirable thing to do?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: It might have been. It could have been done that way. I am not suggesting that the exact procedure adopted was the best one; that is a matter of opinion. We thought that in doing it in the less formal way, as we did originally, we would deal with this matter in Washington on a less formal diplomatic basis and obtain the assurances we thought we had a right to request from the United States. They felt that if we wanted these assurances the first note should be resubmitted as a formal diplomatic note so that we would get a formal diplomatic reply, and that was done.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I believe that the move the minister decided upon in the first place would have been very satisfactory, if it had not been accompanied by the very undesirable headline publicity. That was what bothered the state department.
While speaking this morning in reference to my remarks, the minister spoke as though the government were the only body interested in maintaining the unity of the Canadian forces serving overseas. I should like to refer to my remarks this morning when I said, "if this assignment were to be a permanent one, or if our troops were to be sent outside the theatre of operations, then the protest would have been justified, provided the United Nations commander did not first receive the permission of the Canadian government." In other words, if our forces were to be broken up for anything but a very temporary assignment, or if they were to be sent outside the theatre of operations, of course the Canadian government should be notified, and permission received.
However, I went on to say that, in my opinion, if the duty were a temporary assignment, within the theatre of operations, merely to do our share of the routine chores, then I thought it was almost ridiculous to expect the United Nations commander to follow that same procedure with all sixteen governments who have troops serving under him in the Korean theatre. If he wanted someone for guard duty, or almost any kind of routine duty, it seems to me almost ridiculous that the United Nations commander should have to take the time and trouble to obtain the permission from Canada or Turkey or any of the other countries that have troops serving

Supply-External Affairs in the area before assigning troops to that work. If the commander desired to assign troops to some permanent detail, where they are going to be some months away from their mother formation, or if they were going to be sent outside the theatre of operations, that would be a completely different thing. To me this is something which ties the hands of any commander unnecessarily. I think we must remember the tremendous responsibility which a commander like that has. Just so that we may know where we stand on this matter, does the minister really believe this? If, in future, the duties that the United Nations commander wishes some portion of our troops to perform are in the nature of a temporary assignment, within the theatre of operations, and are simply a matter of routine duty, do the minister and this government feel that on every occasion this government's permission must first be obtained?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that is a matter of opinion. When the hon. gentleman talks about the impossibility and the undesirability of a United Nations commander in the field having to consult sixteen governments before he uses their troops for temporary duty in any way in which he may see fit, that is one way of stating the case. The fact of this situation is that there are, I think, only two governments in Korea-apart from the United States government-which have self-contained forces there to be used there as an entity; other forces are there as small contingents and under the terms of reference under which they were submitted to the United Nations, there may be no mention of the way in which they should be used. They are battalions and even smaller than battalions. We sent a self-contained brigade. As 1 indicated this morning, in making that brigade available to the United Nations for combat duty-and that phrase was used in our submission to the Secretary General-in the directive to the brigadier it was made quite clear that the principle of the separate entity of Canadian forces was at all times to be maintained; and that principle was made clear to the unified command.
It was therefore felt that, before detaching even a small part of this brigade for duty 200 miles behind the front lines where the brigade was stationed, it would have been advisable-as no military consideration was involved-for the unified commander to have apprised the Canadian government of his desire. That was the only point at issue. Now that the exchange has taken place between the two governments, that point has been cleared up in a way which is satisfactory to us and, I think, to the United States government.
[Mr. Hees.l

It is always a difficult problem in combined operations of this kind, especially United Nations operations, to reconcile national interests and international action, as I mentioned the other day. I hope that as a result of this exchange and this clearing of the air that problem will not arise in the future. It is also quite clear that not merely this government but all Canadian governments have attached great importance to the principle of Canadian troops serving under Canadian command and being under Canadian control when they are in combined forces, always subject to considerations of military emergency. In respect of our association with other commonwealth forces in the last war we went to the extent, in this House of Commons, of passing the Visiting Forces Act to make sure it was done in this way.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: There is just one more question I should like to ask the minister and it is this. If in the future we find ourselves called upon to make a protest to an allied government about some matter such as this, does the minister not think that instead of doing it in the way of headlines, it would be preferable to do it between the two governments in a quiet, restrained and unpublicized manner? Which does he think is the best way of carrying out this kind of communication between governments?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I can answer that question only by saying that we should be governed by circumstances. This was a situation which we thought was of far greater interest and importance to Canada than it was to the United States or to the United Nations. We therefore made our public statement in the House of Commons. There may not have been in our minds any idea that that statement would cause the headlines that it actually caused in the United States and would arouse as much interest among the editors of certain newspapers such as the Chicago Tribune, the Patterson press, and the Hearst press as well as the Washington Post. I would not want to lay down any hard and fast rule governing situations of this kind.
I think that in any difference of opinion with a friendly government we must always weigh two factors, namely the protection of our own national interests and the effect that any public discussion and division of opinion would have on the unity and the solidarity of the coalition. Those two factors must be taken into consideration in any statement we make or in any action we take which may not be agreeable to some other member of the coalition. In this particular situation, as this was an important matter of principle although the number of troops involved was small, in order to emphasize this Canadian

interest we decided it would be well to make our statement publicly in the House of Commons.
Having said that, I agree entirely with my hon. friend when he says that we should be extremely careful, in any of these differences we may have, to weigh the effect of a public difference on the unity of the alliance. We are all free countries in this coalition. We have to pay a certain price for freedom. One way in which that price is expressed is in our right to disagree publicly with each other. In doing that we cannot help, on certain occasions, giving ammunition to our enemies. There is no doubt about that. But nevertheless we should not give them any more ammunition or any stronger ammunition than the circumstances make necessary.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to change the subject and to take the opportunity provided by consideration of the minister's estimates to make a few observations concerning an organization that comes within the jurisdiction of the minister's department. It is an organization that has demonstrated cooperation and great achievement throughout the years based on good will and friendship between two great countries, Canada and the United States. I am referring particularly to the international joint commission. I am making these few observations this afternoon because I believe that there are a great many people in Canada who are not aware of the importance of this commission or of the good work that it has done throughout the years, and particularly on account of certain remarks made in certain places and in certain editorials and press comments across this country in connection with the personnel and the functions of the commission.
Before I proceed, Mr. Chairman, I might say that we in this group have a high regard for the functions of the international joint commission and for the way in which it works. This getting together of two countries to assemble facts and evidence and then, as a result of that assembling of facts and evidence, to decide where a structure shall be built for the development of our natural resources to the advantage of the people in both countries in many cases, or in one country or the other, is a clear indication of the type of planning that we in this group believe in.
I understand the major functions of the international joint commission are two in number. The first is the hearing of and dealing with applications received from governments or companies who wish to erect certain structures that will affect the level of waters at the international boundary. The second is in dealing with references made to the commission by the governments of Canada and the
Supply-External Affairs United States for certain investigations. I understand that the first applications for investigations were heard in 1912, or that the first application for hearing before the commission was made at that date. Since that time I understand some 45 hearings have been disposed of by the commission. In a previous debate an hon. member said that there should be an investigation of the work of the international joint commission. I cannot see that point, Mr. Chairman, because anyone who wishes to peruse the evidence placed before the commission in all the hearings since 1912 to this day and the disposal of those hearings would have a very thorough understanding of the function and the work of the international joint commission. I understand that at the present time there are three applications before the commission: one from the government of the United States concerning the dam at Libby, Montana; one from the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company concerning the erection of a dam at Waneta; and one from the city of Minot, North Dakota in the United States, concerning some action that will be taken on certain waters.
So far as investigations are concerned, I understand that eleven have been completed from 1912 to date, and six are still in progress. I mention these things briefly, Mr. Chairman, because I live in a constituency which is very interested in the work of the international joint commission at this time, and has been for some years. It is considering some very great problems of that area. I have had the opportunity to attend hearings in the United States and in Canada. I might say that personally I have been greatly impressed with the work the commission is doing and all the people whom I have met who have had an opportunity of attending these hearings have recognized the great value of the work the commission is doing.
I understand that the investigations still in progress are concerned with the Columbia river basis reference, which was issued on March 9, 1944, an investigation of tremendous importance to the people of southeastern British Columbia; the Sage creek reference of April 8, 1946 and the midwestern watershed reference concerning Waterton and Belly rivers and Souris and Red rivers of January 12, 1948, and the air pollution reference of January 12, 1949; the Saint John river reference of September 28, 1950, and the Niagara Falls reference of October 10, 1950.
I mention these, Mr. Chairman, to place on the record the fact that the commission is now making investigations that concern western Canada, the central provinces and eastern Canada. It is making investigations

Supply-External Affairs of great importance to the Canadian people. In view of the great industrial development and the need for power and the need for agricultural extension, there is no doubt about it that the importance of the work of the international joint commission is increasing from year to year. As a matter of fact, wise decisions on our future development depend to a great extent upon wise decisions made by the commission.
I want to make a brief reference to the personnel of the commission. Who are the people charged with the responsibility of representing Canada on the international joint commission? We are fortunate, Mr. Chairman, in Canada in having the type of personnel on the commission that we have at this time. I am mentioning this fact particularly because I think that well qualified men who make some personal sacrifice to serve Canada, as some members of the commission are doing at this time, should be recognized in this house and in the country. We have as the chairman General McNaughton, whose record in the first world war as a soldier, and in the second world war, was outstanding. He is a scientist, an outstanding engineer and administrator. He was the president of the national research council for some time. Mr. George Spence is the second member of the commission. He was a pioneer farmer in western Canada and has had long experience in the legislature, in parliament and in public affairs. He has shown himself to be an outstanding administrator in the administration of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and wherever he has gone his, shall I say, earthy and practical qualities have been recognized particularly by the farmers who attend the various hearings.
Then we have Mr. Lucien Dansereau, an engineer of long experience with the Department of Public Works, a man of wide experience in the field of public works in Canada and in eastern Canada, and in the administration of matters of that sort. In addition to that we have on the international joint commission a loyal staff. Some of the members have been serving that commission for a good many years. They have given loyal and devoted service. More than that, they are a staff who are particularly interested in the success of the commission's activities and in the work the commission is undertaking.
As I said before, I have had the opportunity of attending some of the hearings, and I have read a good number of reports of the various references and of the applications, and I have thus been able to obtain some knowledge of the work of the international joint commission. There is no


doubt about it, Mr. Chairman, that we in Canada are most fortunate to have the present members acting as members of the Canadian section of the international joint commission. They are doing a great work of great importance on an economical basis. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that a close examination of the figures will show that our international joint commission has performed a greater service at a less per capita cost throughout the years than any other international commission in the world. Knowing these -facts, Mr. Chairman, I am sure that hon. members and the majority of Canadians will join me in paying tribute to the work of the commission in the past and to the excellent work that the international joint commission is doing for Canada today.

Earlier in this session similar attention was drawn to a decision handed down by the international court of justice, supporting a claim by the Norwegian government for the right to define that certain waters be included as territorial waters of the Norwegian government, which before that date had not been included as territorial waters.
In -their submission to the international court of justice the Norwegian government adopted what might also be called a new theory, in that they defined a base line which ran from headland to headland along their coast, and from that baseline westward -they included a zone which they considered was their territorial waters. I might say that the definition of this new territorial water affected the fishermen of the United Kingdom who previously had fished in those waters. Now a very similar problem arises in connection with the territorial waters of Canada, both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific.
I bring this matter to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs at this time because of a recent agreement which has been made, known as the north Pacific fishery agreement, based on the peace treaty recently ratified with Japan. By that fishery treaty, Japan, or Japanese fishermen, agreed to -abstain from fishing salmon, halibut and herring in the north Pacific; but they have the right, as they have always had up to now, of fishing for other species of fish off our Canadian -coast. Not to any great extent have the Japanese in the past availed themselves of that right. But the right exists, and the right has been recognized by the fact that only those three species are included in the abstention clause. There are certain waters on the Pacific coast which one can only define as being inland waters lying between such islands as Vancouver island and the Queen Charlotte islands. They

include such waters as Hecate and Queen Charlotte straits and so on which, in the past, have been regarded as the high seas. They extend for more than three miles from any line drawn which follows the indentations of the British Columbia coast line.
For many years the fishermen of the United States have exercised the historic right of fishing for certain species in the waters between Vancouver island and the mainland, and between the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland. I understand an interdepartmental committee has been set up in order to study this whole question of the definition of territorial waters. I would ask the minister to tell us what progress has been made by that interdepartmental committee in the discussion of this subject, because many departments are affected. I understand however that it is under the general conduct of the Department of External Affairs which, naturally, would be the department most vitally interested. I would ask how active that committee is, how many meetings they have held this year, when the last meeting was held, and what progress is being made.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised a point of both practical and legal importance. The traditional position of Canada and a good many other countries has been, as hon. members know, to recognize the three-mile limit as the limit of territorial waters, though outside that three-mile limit it is usually understood that there would be a jurisdictional area extending farther.
This is an important matter from the standpoint of fisheries. The approach to it usually varies, in certain countries, according to whether the fishermen are inshore or offshore fishermen. There is another aspect of the question the hon. member has touched upon, namely the establishment of inland waters-whether one must follow the indentations of the coast line in establishing the three-mile line, and declare anything outside of that as open sea, or whether one should draw the line from headland to headland.
All these questions were given consideration at the time of the discussions in connection with the fisheries agreement with the United States and Japan. I can only say that if on that occasion we had insisted upon the abandonment of the traditional three-mile zone it might not have been possible to secure an agreement.
However, as the hon. member has pointed out, a decision has recently been handed 55704-221
Supply-External Affairs down by the international court of justice on an appeal from Norway, which does give a nation the right to establish a zone of territorial waters wider than the historic three-mile limit. The implications of the decision are important, and that is one of the matters being studied by the interdepartmental committee. I believe the question has also been considered by the fisheries committee of the house. The interdepartmental committee is an active one but has not yet reported to the government, although we expect to have a report from it before long. Represented on it are the Department of Justice and the Department of Fisheries as well as the Department of External Affairs. I am sorry I am not in a position to tell my hon. friend when we shall have the report, but we hope to have it soon.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will relate more particularly to item 102 in the estimates, which deals with the world health organization. The fifth assembly of the world health organization met in Geneva, Switzerland, this year from May 5 to May 22 inclusive, and I was honoured by being appointed by the government of Canada to the Canadian delegation attending that assembly.
The other delegates were Dr. Oliver Leroux, of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Dr. T. C. Routley, secretary of the Canadian Medical Association, Dr. J. T. Phair, deputy minister of the department of health in the province of Ontario, and Mr. Bruce Williams, representative at the permanent delegation of Canada to the European office of the United Nations.
Hon. members are aware that the world health organization was set up as a permanent independent agency at an international conference in New York in 1946. It is supported by funds, subscribed on an agreed basis by member governments.
WHO has its headquarters at Geneva, Switzerland, with six regional offices. One is in North America, one in South America, another in Europe, another in Africa, one in
3500	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs the eastern Mediterranean and another in the Far East. It gets support from governments in all parts of the world, with the exception of Russia and her satellites. They too belonged to the organization at first, but have later withdrawn their financial support.
WHO is run by a director-general in the person of Dr. Brock Chisholm, a Canadian, along with an executive board of eighteen members, six of whom are elected each year. This year Canada was elected to a seat on this board and will, therefore, have some say in the direction of the organization for the next three years. I may add that, in the voting, 60 nations cast their 'ballots. Two were spoiled, >and Canada got 57 of the 58 votes.
The four years that WHO has been in operation have given ample and positive proof that nations can share common problems and can work together for common solutions, while at the same time retaining their full national sovereignty. In the first four years nations have demonstrated that they are willing when necessary to subordinate their national, regional and ideological interests in order that the great work of WHO may go on.
When health leaders of the nations meet together through WHO, dedicated as they are for the betterment of health of all peoples, they cannot help but make a very vital contribution towards international co-operation 'and good will.
Throughout the centuries health professions have developed and applied principles of co-operation for great humanitarian objectives which transcend geographic, political and social barriers. It is this faith which brought WHO into being.
To state it simply and in its broadest terms, the goal of WHO is to prevent disease and heal the sick.
Discussion of international health appealed to our ancestors of two or three generations ago differently from what it does to us today. It meant to them that there were great killer plagues with which mankind has been afflicted since the very beginning of history. Hans Zinnser wrote a very vivid book entitled "Rats, Lice and History". One chapter deals with the relative unimportance of generals and draws attention to the fact that disease can be a much more effective killer than warfare and that epidemics have done as much to shape the course of history as great military leaders and military campaigns. We have only to read accounts of the bubonic plague, the black death, typhus, smallpox,
IMr. McMillan.]

intestinal diseases, syphilis, et cetera, to know that this was so. If we read history we find that our ancestors had great fear of these epidemics and many accounts are on record of how they tried to avoid disease. But lacking knowledge as to its cause and spread, they had frequent reminders of what epidemics meant in terms of fear, misery and wholesale death.
The first effort to control disease on an international scale took place about the middle of the last century or one hundred years ago. The main emphasis at that time was placed on quarantine, on the efforts to keep diseases outside the boundaries of countries. The opening of the Suez canal precipitated restrictive measures on the part of many European countries. The fear was that the opening of commerce with the east would introduce the bubonic plague, yellow fever and other diseases of that nature into European ports. Quarantine is still sound for certain circumstances, but today because of the advance in preventive medicine there is a well-based hope that a number of the most destructive epidemic diseases can be obliterated or at least suppressed to the point where we need no longer fear them to the same degree.
A new concept of international health was recognized in the formation of the world health organization. It is now accepted as reasonable and proper for those sections of world humanity which possess special health knowledge, skills and devices to share these possessions with their less fortunate fellow men. This is a very important new factor in international health, pioneered it is true by voluntary organizations but now vigorously supported by governments through WHO and the technical assistance programs.
Dr. L. A. Scheele, surgeon general of the United States and president of the WHO, who is retiring this year, said:
It has given structure and consistency to the reverence of human life in this world which has had too many lapses into barbarism.
In the four years of WHO existence there has been a greater reduction of death rates in many countries than in any similar period. Diseases like malaria, yaws, syphilis, smallpox, trachoma, plague and yellow fever are definitely being controlled, while tuberculosis and diseases due to environmental sanitation are also receding. Increased production of food and other goods has already resulted in many countries from the improvement of the health of the people. This has been most marked in large areas now under cultivation because of the scientific eradication of malaria infestation.
If we look over the list of subcommittees of WHO we will realize that much other work

is in progress, though probably with results less dramatic than those mentioned. A partial list would include public health administration, maternal and child health, nutrition, health education, nursing, exchange of scientific information, assistance to educational institutions, sanitary conventions and regulations, biological standardization, drugs that produce addiction, as well as committees on various diseases such as leprosy, tuberculosis, malaria, plague, cholera, poliomyelitis, bilhar-ziasis, et cetera.
The policy of WHO has been to encourage self-health. This is essential for the sound development of any program in preventive medicine. It is felt that if WHO supply the necessary materials and get the program well under way, and if the scheme is soundly conceived, it should then be carried through with local resources. The WHO policy was to require governments receiving assistance, either through the regular WHO program or through the special accounts for technical assistance, to pay certain of the local costs involved. These costs, which did not require the expenditure of foreign currency, included the provision of local services, labour, office space, supplies obtainable within the country, local transportation, postal and telecommunications. Lodgings for the international staff were also to be supplied by the recipient country, but in certain circumstances the director-general could agree to provide lodgings from WHO funds.
At the recent meeting in Geneva much dissatisfaction was expressed with these provisions by certain member countries. On behalf of our delegation I stated that the provisions should not be changed. A committee was set up to reconsider the policies on participation of member states in certain costs incurred by WHO. I was elected chairman of this committee which passed a draft resolution giving the director-general power to assume a whole list of local costs. In presenting the resolution to the whole committee I expressed my opposition, but it carried by a large majority. One clause of the resolution refers it to the 1953 world health assembly. I might say that our delegation debated this at different times and our argument was that if they assumed too great a proportion of the costs in a particular country they would not be able to carry out so many projects.
The Canadian delegation on various occasions objected to the increase of the 1953 budget over that of 1952. There were only two other states actively concerned in maintaining the 1953 budget at the 1952 level, namely, the United States of America and the United Kingdom. The financing of WHO budgets is complicated by the problem of nine inactive members and China which 55704-2211
Supply-External Affairs continue to be assessed. Under current procedures their assessments are not considered available for expenditure.
The budget this year, exclusive of money received from the technical assistance program of the United Nations, is up 11 per cent. The total budget is around $9,823,000. That does not mean that Canada will pay 11 per cent more, although we will pay roughly $9,000 more under the 1953 budget. Besides the budget, there were many other items up for discussion in which the Canadian delegation took an active part. Some of these included the approval of the program for' 1953, publications of the world health organization, the advisability of biennial assemblies,, the advisability of holding assemblies of the* world health organization away from Geneva, the sale of WHO seals, internal administration and bookkeeping, fellowships and many other matters. The Canadian delegation took no active part in the long and acrimonious debates both in committee and in the plenary sessions on "regions undesignated". This came up in connection with Tunisia and Morocco as well as when Turkey wanted to withdraw from the eastern Mediterranean regional jurisdiction. The complaint of a delegate from one country that no regional meetings were being held and the reply of the delegates of a group of other countries that no meetings would be held as long as the first country was a member kept the meeting in prolonged tension. While our delegation took no part in acrimonious debate, yet we offered suggestions on many matters, some of which were adopted. We think we did not fail to take a stand on all vital matters and hope we made a useful contribution to the conference.

I should like the minister to bring us up to date on the situation in the Pacific and on Canada's policy on Pacific affairs. There seems to be less prospect of a truce in Korea although that impression is gained from press reports and may not represent the actual position. Then we would also like to know the situation in the other spots

Supply-External Affairs in Asia where there is fighting, particularly Indo-China and Malaya.
Another development within recent days, in fact I think it took place yesterday, was the recognition by the Japanese government of the Chinese nationalist government as the government for the whole of China. That appears to be a far-reaching step which may have far-reaching effects. It may even affect Canadian policy. Then there is the withdrawal by the United Kingdom of her commercial interests inside red China. That too seems to be quite an important change in the Pacific region.
We should also like to know whether the government is now any more favourably inclined than before to the negotiation of a pact in the Pacific which will serve the same purpose as the North Atlantic pact does in that area. As the minister knows, we have advocated such a pact for several years but the policy adopted has been one of bilateral agreements. There is an agreement between the United States and Japan, another between the United States and the Philippines, and a third between the United States and Australia and New Zealand. Is it the intention that there will only be these bilateral pacts or is there in prospect a wider pact which will set up some kind of defence organization for the Pacific?
I believe that Russia is more apt to make trouble in the Pacific than in the Atlantic. She has a much wider field across the Pacific ocean and seems to have been more aggressive there than in Europe. I am afraid that as a nation we do not appreciate how much trouble can come from the Pacific and, in fact, if a world war comes it may well come from that direction. I noticed reports in the Vancouver press of the last few days indicating that there has been Russian reconnaissance of Alaska and northern Canada by their strategic air force. That may or may not be true but certainly the Pacific is a dangerous spot, and I should like to know what the policy of the Canadian government is at the present time with regard to that great area.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has brought up a very important subject and has touched upon a very important area of the world. The situation there certainly does not seem to be improving to any great extent -that is an understatement-even though in Europe it may be improving in some respects. I welcome the opportunity to say a few words about this area although I have made statements on the subject recently in the house. In that connection it was indicated this morning by the leader of the opposition that we did not have enough opportunity to
[Mr. Green.5

discuss these matters. I took the opportunity of the luncheon recess to find out on how many days we had discussed international affairs, including affairs in the Far East, during this session, and I think the record is such as to disprove the statement that we do not take these matters seriously in the House of Commons in so far as provision of time for their discussion is concerned. There were four separate occasions during this session when a debate on international matters was initiated, and advantage was taken of those occasions by any hon. member who wished to speak on international affairs. Now we are back again, and I do not complain about it a bit, on Far Eastern and Pacific matters.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has asked me to state the position with regard to Korea, Japan, Indo-China, Malaya and-I would have been very surprised indeed if he had not brought this up-a Pacific pact. So far as the situation in Malaya is concerned, if I may start there, there has been some improvement since General Templer took command, but it is still far from stable. The efforts that are being made to stamp out communist banditry are making progress but it is discouraging to realize that only four or five thousand of these bandits in the jungles of Malaya have been able to create this problem which has persisted for so many years. They are able to do it partly because of the nature of the country, the inaccessibility of the areas in which they take refuge, partly because there is a native population which, through fear, intimidation or some ofrer motive, has been helping them, and partly because they have been able to exploit legitimate feelings of nationalism and the desire for a better life. The situation is better but it is far from being satisfactory.
In Indo-China the drain on French resources of men and money continues. I am informed that the military position is better now than it has been for some time. There again one cannot become unduly optimistic because there always remains the possibility of outside intervention of a greater strength than has been the case up to the present time. The most encouraging feature I can think of in the Indo-Chinese situation has been the increased participation of the Viet N"~i government and army in the dangers that face them. As help continues to go to IndoChina, largely from the United States which is playing a very important part in this area of the world where we are defending ourselves against communist aggression, and where once again the United States is the cardinal factor in that defence, the Viet Nam army is assuming a greater share of responsibility. I believe that is an encouraging development. The more the defence of that

country can rest on a government of its own people and an army of its own people, the belter chance there is of keeping communism outside the country.
The situation in Japan has not altered very much since I last spoke on this matter except in relation to the development to which the hon. member referred, and to which reference was made in the press this morning. I should not like to comment on that until I see the actual text of the Japanese government statement. We have not yet received that text. Press accounts indicate that the recognition which was extended to the nationalist government of China by a treaty signed between the two governments has been extended from the area over which the nationalist government now exercises jurisdiction, that is to say Formosa, to the whole of China. If that is actually the case, it is a matter of some importance.
Then I do not need to tell the house that the armistice negotiations in Korea drag on their weary way. I am still of the opinion, and my opinion is shared by a good many people, that it would be a great mistake on our part if we on the western side took any steps to break off these negotiations. If that is to be done, let it be done by the other side. This policy has been adopted by the unified command, and has been put into effect by the representatives of the unified command with persistence and patience, and I think with great intelligence. Nevertheless little if any progress has been made, and I can only echo what the United Kingdom minister of defence-whom we are so happy to have in our country again-said yesterday, that no one can tell, because no one knows, what is in the hearts of the communist negotiators. As I have said before, there is probably a fifty-fifty chance; there may be an armistice or there may not; I do not know. As the talks drag on all the various governments concerned are searching for some way out of what seems to be an impasse in regard to the armistice and indeed what seems to be a difficult situation in Korea generally.
It has been suggested that the United Nations armistice negotiators might be changed, and representatives of other nations included. This might have been a good idea in the early days, and I do not desire to express an opinion on it, but I am inclined to believe with some others that it would not be of any great value today, and might be misinterpreted. If at this stage of the game the composition of the team of negotiators were changed by the addition of representatives from other nations, it might be taken as an indication of distrust in those
Supply-External Affairs negotiators-as though we had to have somebody alonside them to see what they were doing. We have no such distrust.
The situation in regard to prisoners of war, which seems to be the only point which stands between the negotiators and success, has not changed. There has been no progress in respect of the last offer which was made by the unified command. The communist negotiators have treated that offer, which as I said in the house at the time it was made was extremely fair, with ridicule and with violence. This does not necessarily mean that they may not change their minds very quickly. Violence in communist negotiations can almost instantaneously be followed by concessions if the word comes from headquarters to make concessions. So far there is no indication any such word is on the way.
There are other difficulties in connection with Korea. I touched on one of them this morning. There is the difficulty of the prisoners on Koje, which has come up in another connection. This was a most complicated and frightening problem. We may have our own views about it, but at the same time we have to realize that the situation which faced those on the spot, when they were confronted with the necessity of dealing with these prisoners by the thousands, was one of unprecedented complexity. They had to be dealt with at a time when the United Nations forces were retreating and at a time of great military uncertainty, when no one could be sure whether the position in Korea would be held. Thousands of prisoners had to be herded together without sufficient men to guard them. It is quite understandable that they should be thrown on an island and given some-I was going to use the word "freedom"-in their internal management. As it has turned out that has led to unfortunate consequences, but it is easy to be wise after the event. The Americans themselves, who do not hesitate to criticize their own efforts, have done so on this occasion. I think we should realize also however the difficult problem with which they were confronted. Whether or not they have made mistakes, the fact is now that extremely vigorous action has been taken. So far as we can judge the situation on that island of ill omen is quiet, and we must hope that this particular problem has been liquidated.
As to the future, I can only say that all the governments concerned, as I mentioned just a few minutes ago, are now looking for any possible way out of this situation, and especially in regard to what might be done about the prisoners of war. Consideration has been given to whether there might be some

Supply-External Affairs procedure by way of rescreening the prisoners under international control or some device of that kind which would remove the communist fear that the first screening was not fair. If that could be done and some new machinery set up along those lines it might be possible to remove what seems now to be the last obstacle to the armistice.
In making these investigations, however, I suggest we must of necessity insist on one principle, and1 that is that no one who has surrendered to the United Nations forces must be forced back to the country from which he came. The communists in Korea who talk so much about the Geneva protocol have already forced prisoners whom they have taken to join their own forces. They do not appear on any prisoner of war list; that is one of the incongruities of the situation. But whatever they may have done or not done, I suggest that in working out some arrangement for this prisoner of war question we must take our stand that no prisoner who genuinely refuses to go back-and it must be a genuine refusal1 given to somebody who is capable of interpreting the prisoner's wishes-should be forced back.
This is my final word. If armistice negotiations should break down and be succeeded by another all-out offensive on the part of the communists, the persons responsible- and I repeat what I have said before-should have it made clear to them that the consequences of a second all-out aggression might be far-reaching indeed, even farther reaching than the first.

Israel is not only an Asiatic state in which democracy is practised and western techniques are dynamic; it is already a valuable customer of Canada. Probably the best evidence of the proper use of moneys advanced to assist in the development of underdeveloped countries is contained in the report of the secretary of the export-import bank with headquarters in Washington. Sidney Sherwood, the secretary of the export-import bank, in a short article under the heading "Making the Most of a Loan", wrote as follows. I should like to quote his words because I think they contain the germ of further worth-while ideas. He wrote:
In January of 1949, the export-import bank loan to Israel was made in the amount of $100 million to assist the new state in carrying out its economic development program. This loan to Israel was made only after long and thorough study of the economic risks involved.
He goes on later to say:
In fact, the export-import bank with $3 billion in outstanding loans or undisbursed commitments in over forty countries has few borrowers who have used their loan dollars more wisely or meticulously than has Israel.
The final report of the United Nations economic survey mission for the Middle East states:
The case of Israel is sui generis. There one finds a western civilization of the most modern type which is making prodigious efforts to draw life from the barren soil of Palestine.
In this age of transition when all over the world not only political ideologies but economic patterns are in sharp conflict, it is no wonder that eyes are being increasingly focused on the Middle East in a sharp concentration on the impact of all of the forces which plague the modern world.
Here we find the conflict of past and present. In Israel western civilization has been injected into a region dominated by an eastern, semi-feudalistic system of land-tenure. In Israel socialism and co-operative enterprise are working hand in hand and side by side with private enterprise for the development of a new economy.
Is it possible that the resolution of the problems concentrated in this small but strategic part of the world will provide patterns for solutions on a wider scale? If the experiments now being carried on in Israel and the Arab states succeed in finding a modus vivendi, history may well record that the Middle East played the role of the crossroads laboratory of civilization in one of the greatest crises the world has known.
This is a critical moment for the new state of Israel. Canadians have a strong cultural attachment with the peoples of Israel. We have already, especially in the United Nations, proved our friendship for that country. Now when Israel needs help to meet

Consequently I would ask the minister to give some attention to this very item, and see if there is not something more we as a Canadian nation can do to help one of our really good friends in the Middle East.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
We may even get what I am asking for.
The republic of Austria occupies a key position geographically in Europe. Not only does Austria occupy a key position geographically but she is still an occupied country with Russian troops actually on her soil. She is still very much in the forefront of the war that is not cold by any manner of means, certainly as far as the Russian occupied portion of the city of Vienna goes.
I again want to make a plea for recognition by the appointment of a Canadian minister to Vienna. I do that for a number of reasons. First of all, if Austria and her really amazing fight against engulfment by communism can be recognized, we will help to make her a strong as well as a free and independent country.
There is, and there always must be, a great cultural tie between Austria and Germany. They are both Germanic peoples. There is also a tremendous economic tie. It was, if I may say so, the stupidity of France in the twenties in opposing the proposed economic union which eventually sowed the seeds of the national socialist party in Austria and which eventually resulted in the putsch and the taking over of Austria by Hitler.
It must be remembered that the first real act of extraterritorial aggression by Hitler was against the sovereign state of Austria, and there is still a danger of regarding Austria as an adjunct of Germany. I would hope that as soon as possible our government will appoint a minister to Vienna. There are many excellent reasons for this, entirely apart from the geographical position of Austria. Three times before in history the very frontier which is being defended now was defended against the Asiatic horde. I had the privilege of being near Vienna, in the American zone on the Danube, and seeing the Americans manning positions. One of the officers showed me a mound near one of their posts which had been a Roman fortification nearly 2,000 years ago. 

Looking down from Kobenzl over Vienna one saw Russian barracks in almost exactly the same place as the Turkish encampments when Prince Sobieski, in September 1683, threw back the Mongol hordes. Those are historical incidents which are being repeated today. From our point of view we should do everything possible to recognize Austria as a sovereign nation, not as a territory to be serviced from our embassy or our legation in Berne, and certainly not as an adjunct of our embassy in Bonn. The minister may have done something about this in the last few weeks. If so I am glad to hear of it as Vienna is again the outpost of Christian and western civilization.
There is one other thing I should like to see done, and here again I may not be fully informed as to what may have happened. I refer to the procedure in providing asylum to the escapees. I think the attorney general of the United States, Francis Biddle, was prominent in the organization which looks after escapees from communist countries. Up to comparatively recent times the escapee would come over from the communist country. He would escape luckily with his life. Of course he would have no papers, and frequently very little identification. Because he had no papers and little identification, the first thing that would happen to him would be this. He would be put in prison until such time as he could get papers or other identification, which often was never. In other words, immediately he made his escape he was kept at a frontier point, in a state of imprisonment. There is of course a very obvious danger that many of the escapees may be plants; they may be Russian agents or communist agents escaping for that purpose, but I feel that there are methods by which we can weed out those who are in that category. I realize there is great difficulty in doing that. I would like to know what we are doing to see, so that these men who have had the courage to escape from the communist world, whatever part it may be, are looked after by some organization. I know our record in that respect has been good. As a matter of fact, until comparatively recent years our record was considerably better than that of the United States. We were prepared to take many of these people without all the documentation asked by the United States. I feel that is one of the worth-while things that can be done today in Europe, to assist our friends from behind the iron curtain, to obtain physical safety and political asylum.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
In regard to the first point, we appreciate as does the hon. member the importance of Austria at this time-indeed especially at this time. We have been discussing with the Austrian government the possibility of an exchange of diplomatic

representatives. I hope to be able to make an announcement on the subject before long, though I cannot be sure that it will completely satisfy the hon. member.
Then with reference to the question of escapees, as the hon. member has indicated I believe it can be said that we have played some part in giving asylum to these unfortunate people some of whom have done so much for freedom, for democracy and for us. There is always the consideration of security, and it is a specially important consideration in these cases because, as the hon. member has suggested, this is the kind of thing that could be exploited by those desiring to bring people into our country for wrong purposes. However, once security considerations have been met, we have made special arrangements on occasions to take escapees into Canada, and I hope we will continue to discharge our share of that international duty.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: I gather that every case is judged on its merits; there is no special organization looking after escapees?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: No, there is no special organization; but we have established contact with the committee to which my friend has referred. Then, of course, we are also participating in the new refugee organization, PICMME, that is continuing the work of IRO. Through that organization we are in touch with some of them.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND

speechtext:
Arising out of the minister's reply to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra when he asked about Formosa, I should like to ask a further question. I realize the minister's statement was necessarily brief. I realize, too, that there was no real need for him to repeat statements he had made before. It does strike me, however, that the statement he made today was a little too brief. All he said was that, so far as Formosa is concerned, it is the seat of the Chiang Kai-shek government, which the Canadian government still recognizes.
I trust-and this is my reason for rising at this time-that there is no change on the government's part in the position the minister indicated to the house earlier in this session. That was a repetition of the position he stated on previous occasions, but he gave it again on March 21, 1952, when, after making certain other statements, he said:
We do not intend to use our own forces to restore to China the regime which is now in Formosa after being driven off the mainland.
I trust the statement the minister made today, that the Chiang Kai-shek government on the island of Formosa is a government recognized by the Canadian government, does 55704-222
Supply-External Affairs not mean that this government is showing any interest in Chiang Kai-shek being restored to the mainland of China.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
No. There is no change whatever in our position. And if any statement of mine this afternoon implied that there was, I would like to correct that implication. However, I do not think what I said is susceptible of that interpretation. If I remember correctly, I said we recognized Formosa as being under the jurisdiction of Chiang Kai-shek and, as such, part of China. It is de facto part of China. The final disposition of Formosa has not yet been determined; but it has always been viewed by this government in the light of international arrangements which had previously been agreed upon.
So far as any action is concerned on our part to restore the nationalist Chinese regime on Formosa, our attitude in that matter is exactly as it was stated last March.

Supply-External Affairs

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: If I remember rightly we adhered to that Cairo declaration, and we also are committed to some extent by the terms of the peace declaration with Japan. subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND

speechtext:
I understood the minister to say this morning that he is responsible for everything taking place in his department. I shall now make reference to something affecting his department, and then he will be free to judge whether or not he has been responsible for this condition.
In the last six months I have had considerable contact with the passport office. I must say that I would not have had this contact had not people written to me to obtain passports. You would think they could be picked up in about five seconds.
I should like to give the details of one case. Twenty-five years ago an immigrant from Denmark settled in Prince Edward Island. After he had been there a short time he married a fine lady and started in as a citizen of our province, taking out his naturalization papers five years later. He was quite successful in life, and only about two weeks ago decided to take a trip back to his homeland. He wanted to take his wife along. He made application to the passport office, but before doing so he paid for his transportation via New York.
Mr. J. W. O'Brien, a passport officer, sent the husband his passport' but wrote to the wife stating in a very nice letter that when she had married she had given up her citizenship. He explained to her that she would have to get a registration certificate from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. That is where I came into the picture. I got a long letter from these people telling me they were afraid they might lose their fare. I immediately telephoned to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and I sent over their letter at once by messenger.
The matter was taken up immediately and this lady in Charlottetown was told to fill out and sign certain papers and return them, after
fMr. Mackenzie.]

which a certificate would be issued immediately. The gentleman in that department
said he would take it over immediately to the passport office. I want to say that this gentleman, Mr. J. E. Duggan, and Mr. O'Brien both indicated that they were ready to do everything they could to provide service to the people who were requesting it. After dealing with them I have come to the conclusion that if there are two civil servants who are ready to do more under trying circumstances I would like to meet them.
Just one other incident I should like to mention. I wanted a small favour from the minister of external affairs. I knew he was a busy man, so I saw a Mr. Molson in his office. I want to say that I have never received better service from anyone since coming to Ottawa. I just wanted to place on record my appreciation of the courtesy extended by these three gentlemen. I leave it to the minister to say whether he is responsible or not.

speechtext: I wonder if under this item the minister could make a statement on Canada's part in the United Nations disarmament commission?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I can make a statement and I hope to be able to keep it fairly brief. The disarmament commission, which was set up at the last assembly of the United Nations, has been quite active with meetings in New York. The Canadian representative on that commission is our permanent representative to the United Nations, Mr. David Johnson. In fact he was the chairman of the disarmament commission in the first month of its existence.
We had hoped that this commission might be the means of providing a sincere and constructive effort to reduce the level of armaments, but from the very beginning the delegate of the U.S.S.R. removed most of the hope we had of that purpose being achieved because he used the commission as a sounding board to attack the United States, especially in regard to the fantastic charge of germ warfare in Korea.
It is true that the U.S.S.R. did put forward their usual scheme for the immediate reduction of all armed forces. This scheme has been analysed, and we have tried to show them that it would not work. However, it was not considered desirable to take merely 55704-222J
Supply-External Affairs a negative attitude in this commission so the United Kingdom, the United States and the French members of the commission, in consultation with Canadian and other members, put forward a proposal of their own for arms reduction. It was thought that it was a practical one and could be taken as a basis for consideration. It was in a sense an effort to meet the Russian position, and it established the level of the armed forces of the U.S.S.R. and the United States at 1,500,000 men, of China I believe at 1,500,000 men, of France and the United Kingdom at 750,000 each, and with respect to other countries in the proportion of 1 per cent of their population. This was put forward by these delegates in good faith. It was hoped that it might be examined by the U.S.S.R. as a sincere and constructive proposal, but since then it has been turned down by the U.S.S.R. representative on the commission, and for the time being that has made progress difficult, if not impossible. However, the commission is not giving up and will continue to meet and report to the next session of the assembly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: I wish to express the hope that every use that can be made of this commission and other means in the propaganda battle will be used. We are getting into a state where we have various kinds of war and various kinds of peace. Amongst the wars we have are cold war, hot war and propaganda war. I suggest there are times when we do seem to let the other side take a little of the initiative in the propaganda for the reduction of armaments and for peace. I simply express the hope that we will not always let the other side make these moves first and leave us in the position of having to try to counteract them, but that on occasion we will use a commission such as this to make propaganda moves ourselves.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: I agree. That was one of the reasons why so much time and effort were put into the proposal of the three western powers which I have just mentioned and which is still before the commission.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I do not want to be one of those who sneer at international organizations, because I believe in them very greatly. On the other hand, one does feel that it is very easy for them just to grow and grow if we say nothing about them. Here we have the food and agriculture organization which is costing us $135,000 more. Would the minister say a word about that? Actually it is costing us more than double this year.

Supply-External Affairs

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
The representatives of the Department of Agriculture could more effectively describe the operations of this United Nations specialized agency, but I can say that it is considered by those who have had something to do with it, and who have had something to do with other United Nations organizations, as one of the most practical and useful of the specialized agencies of the United Nations. The technical divisions of the food and agriculture organization through which it does its work are agriculture, distribution, commerce and statistics, forestry and fisheries, nutrition and rural welfare.
During the first five years of its operation FAO has established a statistical service in the fields of food and agriculture and forestry and fisheries. It has collected, collated and published a wide range of technical information. It has also-and I think this is the most important part of its work-assisted participating countries, especially what we call underdeveloped countries, in improving the efficiency of their food production by providing them with technical advice and assistance for various periods of time and by sending technical agricultural missions to those countries. Canadian experts have taken part in a good many of these missions.
FAO has also -undertaken a number of experimental projects in the field under its terms of reference. One that occurs to me was in Mexico where, by virtue of an FAO mission and the assistance FAO was able to give to that country, the production of a certain agricultural commodity was increased many times with great value to Mexico. I think it is doing a useful and practical job the value of which, of course, as is so often the case in these matters, is much greater to countries less materially advanced than to those like Canada which are materially advanced in agriculture. I can only conclude by saying that I think the money we spend on the food and agriculture organization is well spent.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: As the minister described it, it reminded one, though with differences, of the Colombo plan. I suppose there is a very marked difference. The Colombo plan, I take it, does not deal directly with food but with mechanical installations of various kinds. I suppose that first of all the Colombo plan is not a United Nations plan but a commonwealth plan, and I take it there is a great distinction there. The minister spoke of FAO being able to do useful and constructive work in Mexico. I take it that was merely by way of advice. I suppose FAO has no -means of stepping in and giving material assistance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: In the case of the Mexican venture which I mentioned they did in fact send a technical agricultural mission to Mexico which stayed there some time and was responsible to a very large extent for the increased production. It also used facilities placed at its disposal by the government of Mexico. The Colombo plan of course works in co-operation with FAO whenever any project under the Colombo plan needs agricultural experts or agricultural assistance. That has happened once or twice already.

speechtext: I should like to ask the minister whether FAO has arrived at a position any nearer to the acceptance of such an organization as an international commodity clearing house for the proper distribution of world surpluses of food.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: May I ask the minister what seems to be the main difficulty in the way of establishing a scheme that would be acceptable. Is it finance?

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
