subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: That would be a matter of finance, would it not?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Oh, well, Mr. Chairman,
finance enters into all these matters. That is quite true.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I realize that the minister is in a difficult position in dealing with this matter. Human common sense would dictate that mankind should believe that where we can produce an abundance of goods we should somehow or other be able to get them into the hands of people who want to use them. My general idea concerning FAO at its inception was that the men who conceived the idea intended to accomplish exactly that. They said that if man can produce the goods then it is our business to be able to put them into the possession of the people who want to consume them. In other words if the world can produce enough food, clothing and shelter, it is a complete anomaly that 1,500 million

people should go to bed hungry every night.
It is our business to devise ways and means whereby that production of which the world is capable shall supply the needs of such unfortunate people. Do I get the impression that the minister thinks that was the idea behind the FAO?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: I cannot really add very much to what I have said on this matter. As some hon. members will recall, this question was discussed in some detail before the standing committee on external affairs. There is an FAO committee on commodity problems. It is meeting now, and is going to correlate the needs of the various agricultural organizations. The Canadian representatives on that committee are I believe Dr. Barton and Dr. Hudson. A report on the work of the committee up to the present was given to the standing committee on external affairs. If hon. members are interested, they will find it as an appendix to the minutes and proceedings of the committee, No. 3. The report of the FAO committee on commodity problems has outlined some of the difficulties in the way of success in this field, but FAO is endeavouring to make progress.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I have just a word to say, Mr. Chairman, in connection with this same item. I should like to say that the reason I asked the question was this. Since we examined the estimates in the external affairs committee a report was issued by one of the agencies of United Nations, I believe on May 12, indicating in some detail the conditions in the world with respect to food. I believe one of the important statements made in the report was that, in the opinion of the committee, if all the factors, land, fertilizer, modern machinery and the technical knowhow throughout the world were to be utilized fully, there is no question about the ability of the world to produce sufficient food to take care of the needs of 2,400 million people. It is believed that they could be fed and kept at a fairly good standard of well-being.
That being the case, I have wondered about our own situation in Canada. We are not producing anything like the amount of food we could produce. Our farmers are afraid to go all-out in their productive efforts because they cannot find a market. If they did make that all-out effort they would find, under present circumstances at any rate, that present prices would be depressed so badly they just could not stay in business. It does seem to me a sad state of affairs that our producers of food in this country are not making an effort, and that inducements are not held out to them to enable them to
Supply-External Affairs produce all the food the world needs and yet stay in business. This is especially true when one considers the statement of the hon. member for Lethbridge that nearly half of the world's population is forced to go to bed hungry every night. We come face to face with the paradox of the world's, abundance on the one hand, and on the other the suffering and deprivation on the part, of half the people.
Because I have thought a good deal about that since that report was issued, I asked the-question about the international commodity clearing house. It seems to me that such a body is not only desirable but absolutely essential if we are going to be able to furnish these people in backward countries and underprivileged areas with the things they need. It seems to me now is the time to be pushing this just as hard as we possibly can.
While I am saying something about this work, I should like to mention the services of the gentleman who made his report in the external affairs committee, Mr. Nik Cavell. I believe his services had been utilized in connection with technical assistance. I am sure the minister will not mind my mentioning it at this point, but I heard his report and had an opportunity to question him in the committee. I must say that Canada is fortunate in having a man of his ability and wide experience to administer our share of the technical assistance being advanced to the underprivileged and underdeveloped areas of the world. I was deeply appreciative of the fine job this man has done, and I wanted to say a word before the committee. I believe we are very fortunate in having a man of his calibre engaged in this work.
When we come to item 108 I hope the minister, in answering a plea that was made on behalf of Israel this afternoon by the hon. member for Mount Royal, will mention what plans are now in the process of formulation for increasing the amount of assistance to these underprivileged areas, and whether it is possible for him to use more money, and use it wisely and efficiently, than is being provided at the moment.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
I do not wish to hold matters up, but it seems to me that in this problem which has been raised there lies the whole secret of the decision as to whether or not we are going to win the peace. It is a foregone conclusion which must be obvious to every thoughtful person inside this house and out, that we cannot reasonably expect conditions of peace to prevail in a world in which 1,500 million people have to go to bed

Supply-External Affairs hungry every night. In a world which the great Creator has abundantly provided with the means of production of all the goods which are necessary to give everyone in the world a reasonable standard of living, I do not think we can afford to let this matter slip by without a considerable amount of emphasis in our expression concerning the question.
I realize that the minister is quite helpless in this matter. Nevertheless it comes up for discussion under his estimates. It is just one of the headaches, of which he has an abundant supply.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: Tell him how to fix it up.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
Yes, I shall tell him how to fix it up. As a matter of fact, in my speeches in this house during the last two years I have laid down a definite policy to fix it up. There has been no criticism of the suggestions I have made, nor intelligent questioning of those suggestions. I shall challenge anybody in this house to offer any criticism.
It is quite obvious that the difficulty is financial. The FAO organization, no matter how it may try, under the present financial system just cannot possibly get the money with which to buy from Canada, as an example, the surplus goods that Canada can produce and render available for distribution in the world. Now, is that not putting the matter simply, in a nutshell? That is the problem, is it not?

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
How do you solve that problem? What we are trying to do is to tax Canada, in addition to all the other taxes we are laying on, for the FAO. Under our present financial system we are forced to tax Canada for enough additional money to provide the FAO with enough money to enable the FAO to buy the surplus products of Canada. Is that not plainly and simply put? In respect of the United States, FAO under the present financial system has to call on the United States to tax the United States for enough additional money to provide FAO with enough dollars to buy the surplus products the United States is capable of fabricating and rendering available for distribution in the world. Is that not putting it straight?
The problem is this. Canada cannot afford that taxation. The United States cannot afford that taxation. If those two nations cannot afford it, no other nation can. Then how in the world are we going to enable FAO to obtain the money with which to buy the surplus production these two nations alone are capable of fabricating? That is the question simply put. tMr. Blackmore.]

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: The hungry countries have no money and they have nothing to exchange.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: That is right. Therefore do we say that because they have nothing to exchange, they must die?

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: Not necessarily. But you have to tax somebody to pay your producers for the goods.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: But you cannot tax the people who produce them; and it is a foregone conclusion that you cannot tax the people who have to consume them, because those potential consumers are already in the depths of poverty.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext: So where do we go from there?

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
That is the question. Where do we go from there? The answer must be found in what social credit has proposed time and time again for seventeen solid years in this house, namely that nations must be prepared to create money debt free and render that money available. Let us take the United States as an example. The United States could create money by the billions, debt free, in order to buy her own surplus of production. A number of people may say, "That will not work." But, Mr. Chairman, the fact is that we have found out that nothing which has been proposed up to the present time can possibly work. If the solution is to be found, it must be along the line of creating debt free dollars.
Could the United States safely create $1 billion of United States money and put it into the hands of FAO, to be used for the purchase and distribution of United States goods among needy nations? The answer is a resounding yes. All United States history and all financial history proves it beyond any shadow of doubt, if we will clear away the prejudice which has been engendered in our minds by men who have endeavoured to keep us enslaved. Abraham Lincoln created $450 million of greenbacks in the civil war. With those dollars he won the war. It now remains to be shown why the United States administration today could not create a corresponding amount of money, debt free, and either give it to FAO or put it in the hands of the needy nations so they can buy American goods.
The greatest problem that faces the United States and Canada today is that of markets, the problem of being able to get rid of their goods. I do not wish to bear down on this subject too long, Mr. Chairman, but I think the House of Commons should require the minister to determine exactly why FAO is unable to do the thing it ought to do-and

which everybody's common sense tells him it. ought to do-and then, the next time he comes before the house, be prepared to give not a shifty, evasive, meaningless answer but a factual answer that will meet the demands of intelligent minds.
I do not propose to enlarge on this subject because probably it would not be quite in order for me to do so. On the other hand I do not know but that it is the thing which is most in order under this item. If an arrangement could be made among the nations-the United States, Canada, Britain, France, the members of NATO and all the other nations that are able to produce and that want to purchase and want to sell- for determining some means whereby money could be created and rendered available for buying and distributing surplus goods, there is no reason under the sun why such a proposal should not succeed. It will be the greatest single factor contributing to peace just as the lack of it now is the greatest single factor contributing to war. For us to pretend that we can seriously go about the problems of removing the causes of war without attacking this essential matter of money for distributing surplus goods is to make ourselves ridiculous in the eyes of all realistic people.
Last year I suggested-and with this comment I will close at the present time unless I am provoked to go on a little further-that we could easily make Great Britain the clearing house. The hon. member for Cape Breton South will readily appreciate this suggestion. We could easily make Great Britain the clearing house if we and the United States would get off Great Britain's back, and abolish our contemptible unconditional most favoured nation clause and our GATT arrangement and all the others that have been strangling our commonwealth, and in place of them take effective measures to make Britain strong as she should be by now, so long after the war. Great Britain can create pounds sterling. There is no question about the remarkable success of the pound sterling, is there? There is no reason under the sun why Great Britain cannot create pounds sterling and distribute those among these unfortunate nations, take from us the goods which are necessary to enable her to support such pound sterling issues and become a great factor in the distribution of goods in the world. If there is anyone in the country who can offer a reason for questioning what I have said, I hope he will get into this chamber and give the reason. I am challenging anyone to show that the method of approach which I have suggested would not succeed.
Supply-External Affairs
Most of those nations that are now "have not" nations can produce certain kinds of goods and offer them for sale. Let us take Japan as an example. There is no nation on the earth that is potentially a better producer than is Japan. There are no people who are more skilful, more adaptable and more willing to work than are the Japanese people. Yet when they produce and then offer their goods to the world, they confront an almost impassable barrier because we refuse to accept their goods, What is the way out of all that difficulty? If Britain could take raw materials from raw material producing nations and exchange those with the Japanese for the goods they are able to produce, and then place those Japanese goods in the nations where they are needed and receive their production in return, it is conceivable that it would not be long-probably four or five years-until you would have built up in Britain an organization as a result of which the whole world trade could begin to be integrated and you would have real multilateral trade.

The answer to that question must be a resounding yes. Then why in the name of common sense can we not provide the people who need textiles with the means of buying the textiles that the textile industries of the world stand ready and eager to produce? That is the question. I submit that if there is any member in the house who would give a realistic answer to that question, that answer must be yes. I thank the hon. member for his question. The same thing would be true in respect of all other goods.
For a further example, is there any conceivable reason, as the hon. member for Peace River has pointed out, why we today in Canada should be reducing or limiting our production of hogs when 1,500 million suffering people require food? We are discouraging the production of cheese, of milk, of eggs, of fruit and a great number of other commodities. We ask: Are we discouraging their production? Of course we are, because we say there are no markets. Well, there are people needing these foods, hundreds of millions of them. People are dying because they cannot get the foods. A food and agriculture organization has been set up to take care of that very problem, and the item providing for the support of that organization is under discussion before us at this moment. What are we going to do about it? I submit that until the Secretary of State for External Affairs calls on the members of the Canadian cabinet and says:	Gentlemen, we just cannot fool with this thing any longer. speechtext: I want to raise again with the minister the question I raised before. The international labour organization was established in 1919 at the time of the establishment of the league of nations. It was an independent organization; and it has continued to do useful work. speechtext:
The international labour
organization is a specialized agency of the United Nations, even though it was established long before the United Nations. Actually it was established in the time of the old league of nations, as my hon. friend recalls. It has been very active since the war. A number of international labour conferences have been held which representatives of employers, employees and governments attended; there have been various trade committee meetings held. About 200 conventions and recommendations have been adopted, dealing with wages, hours of work, employment of women and children, labour conditions in special industries and things of that kind. I think these conventions have been useful. There again the situation is very much like that of FAO. The usefulness of this organization is greater in countries where labour standards are not as highly developed as they are in our own country. But I think it is a useful international organization. It is certainly considered as such by the labour organizations of this country, and I hope this vote for the continuance of Canadian support will be accepted by the committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND

speechtext: What are the functions of the economic committee? The amount involved is small, but I would like to know what it is for.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT BY DR. ENDICOTT
speechtext:
This is a commonwealth committee which originated from one of the resolutions of the imperial economic conference of 1923. It has continued in existence ever since, though now on a much reduced scale of activity. There was some question after the war as to whether certain of these commonwealth committees, which had not been very active, should be re-established. It was decided to re-establish this committee but to keep its activities down to a minimum so that, if it could be used for purposes of expansion later on, as work developed^ it would be available.
I must confess there has not been much for it to do since the war. On the other hand its expenses are limited. It does issue volumes of what it calls a commodity series, setting out statistics in regard to world production, commonwealth production and commonwealth trade. It has also been issuing certain periodical intelligence services which are published sometimes weekly and sometimes monthly, as necessity indicates. This is an intelligence service in respect of trade in certain commodities within the commonwealth. That is about the extent of its activities.

subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND

Mr. Chairman, in this connection I fancy people throughout the country who read Hansard will be interested in the following figures. Canada this year can afford $1,463,200 for the United Nations
(Mr. Pearson.]
Organization; she can afford $246,800 for FAO; she can afford $248,900 for the international labour organization, and $331,800 for UNESCO. But for the commonwealth economic committee she can afford only 16,830 measly dollars.
That is something to arouse a person's interest. We know the greatness the British commonwealth had attained up to world war I. We know the British commonwealth almost single-handed, with the assistance of France and Russia, held the Kaiser at bay. We know the British commonwealth held Hitler at bay. One of the greatest stabilizing factors the world over, not only from the military but from the economic standpoint, was the British commonwealth. Why in the world is it we have lost interest in the British commonwealth? What has gone wrong with the puny men who are guiding us today? What are the powers behind them that are making them act like this? Surely what the British commonwealth was it is capable of becoming again; it has the same people and the same resources.
Why was there any doubt as to whether or not this economic committee should continue? I will tell you why. The policy, the concepts of men in the Canadian government and in the other governments that had to do with all this whole thing were guided by a group of evil people who wanted to destroy the British commonwealth. Why do they want to destroy the British commonwealth? Because the British commonwealth has been too great a blessing to mankind, in the minds of those evil people who are guiding the destinies of the world right now-from the United States. The thing we have to face up to right now is whether we are going to allow these evil forces to continue to weaken the British commonwealth and disintegrate it as they have already gone far towards doing, or whether we are going to have the British commonwealth rise and become the great and mighty power it ought to be in this year 1952, and which it can be if the Canadian government and other governments in the empire stand solidly together and say to the United States, "you have gone just as far as you are going to go in this matter of destroying the British empire".
I say that next time the minister should bring down probably ten times as large a vote for this economic committee, and I hope he will do other things to change the ideas of certain people. I still believe there is a great deal of virtue in that fine song about Britain which goes: "God, who made thee mighty, make thee mightier yet". That applies to the British commonwealth if we

have the wisdom and courage to apply it. So will the minister just see that this economic committee is supported more generously in the future and be ready to bring in a report next time which will go much further than just telling us about a few pamphlets of statistics published?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN TROOPS ON KOJE ISLAND

It was also decided that Canada's contribution toward that $100,000 would be about 16 or 17 per cent, and that percentage is reflected in this vote. That is all there is to it.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 17, consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation -Mr. Larson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first time in nearly two years that I have made a statement on one of these bills which are presented to us for the purpose of incorporating a pipe line company. I do so for the purpose of indicating my opposition to this particular application and to the procedure which is followed in dealing with matters of this kind. In fact, my remarks are as much directed to the procedure as to the specific purpose of the bill before us. There is no pretence whatever that the purpose of this discussion is anything else than the hope that it will not be possible to deal with this bill during this session. After all, that should be frankly stated. It is the only device that can be employed to prevent the passage of a measure which certain members think should not pass, and where it appears that there is to be no real attempt to place before the house any sound argument in favour of the adoption of the bill that has been presented.
I have listened to the arguments that have been made against the adoption of this measure. I think those arguments are sound.
I think the arguments should appeal to the judgment and common sense of the members. There has been no serious attempt on the part of anyone to meet the arguments that have been put forward. The attitude seems to be simply this: The bill is before the house, and we are not going to say anything more. We hope you will not be able to keep on talking against the measure and that in due course, without any argument in its support, it will come to a vote and we are sure that a majority will support it. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is a reflection on the whole house. I suggest it is a reflection on the methods of this house, and it is a reflection on the manner in which the members are called upon to deal with what should be serious business.
My remarks are prompted particularly by the fact that when this bill was before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, the evidence from expert witnesses who were available was cut off arbitrarily by a motion presented to that committee. On Thursday, April 24 of this year, at a meeting of that standing committee the hon, member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) moved that sufficient evidence had been obtained for the committee to

decide as to the economic practicability of the pipe line under consideration, and that the question be put on the preamble without further examination of the witness. After discussion and the question having been put on the motion, it was agreed to on division. The record of the committee then sets out the division, and I see that the motion was supported by a substantial majority. The members of the opposition opposed it, with the support of one Liberal member of that committee.
That motion was not only to the effect that other witnesses should not be heard, but that the committee had heard enough from a particular witness. That witness was a man who was giving reasons why he thought it was not sound economically and otherwise to proceed with this particular pipe line. That course having been adopted, and the House of Commons now being asked to pass a bill which was denied an adequate examination before the committee, I do not think that the members of the house, without the opportunity to hear witnesses, should be called upon to deal with it.
I wish to speak about the procedure. I hope the extended discussion which has taken place on this measure may serve to impress upon the government the desirability of another procedure in dealing with the issuing of charters for pipe-line companies. I think it is appropriate to review exactly what it is the House of Commons is being asked to support by the motion now before us. We start with the fact that this bill is to incorporate a pipe-line company under the Pipe Lines Act which was passed by the House of Commons on April 30, 1949. That act, which is the overriding act empowering pipe-line companies to carry on their corporate activities, gives certain powers to any company incorporated to operate a pipe line. I think the members of the house should recognize how far they are being asked to go when they support a measure of this kind. Section 7 of the Pipe Lines Act sets out the powers which automatically are conferred upon any company which receives incorporation in this manner and then obtains authority to proceed with pipe-line activities by permission of the government and the board of transport commissioners who must pass upon the application.
I wish to read these into the record because they indicate the extremely wide powers that any such corporation receives. I am inclined to think hon. members generally have not been impressed with what it is they are being called upon to do. Section 7 of the Pipe Lines Act reads as follows:
7. A company may. for the purposes of its undertaking, subject to the provisions of this act and the special act.
Boundary Pipeline Corporation
(a)	enter into and upon any crown land without previous licence therefor, or into or upon the land of any person, living in the intended route of its line, and make surveys, examinations or other necessary arrangements on such land for fixing the site of the line, and set out and ascertain such parts of the land as are necessary and proper for the line:
(b)	purchase, take and hold of and from any person any land or other property necessary for the construction, maintenance and operation of its line and alienate, sell or dispose of any of its land or property that for any reason has become unnecessary for the purpose of the line;
(c)	construct, lay, carry or place its line across, upon or under the land of any person on the located line of the company pipe line;
(d)	join its line with the pipe line of any other person at any point on its route;
(e)	construct, erect and maintain all necessary and convenient roads, buildings, stations, depots, wharves, docks and other structures, and construct, purchase and acquire machinery and other apparatus necessary for the construction, maintenance and operation of its line;
(f)	construct, maintain and operate branch lines, and for that purpose exercise all the powers, privileges and authority necessary therefor, in as full and ample a manner as for a company pipe line;
(g)	from time to time alter, repair or discontinue the works or any of them, mentioned in this section, and substitute others in their stead;
(h)	transport oil or gas by company pipe line and regulate the time and manner in which oil or gas shall be transported, and the tolls to be charged therefor; and
(i)	do all other acts necessary for the construction, maintenance and operation of its line.
Those are immensely wide powers, Mr. Chairman; yet those are the powers which automatically are conferred by the Pipe Lines Act upon any company which receives a charter under a bill such as that which is now before the house. I do not think hon. members should be asked to confer powers of that kind under which they can seize property that we do not even know yet by actual description. If this company is incorporated and if it should receive the permission of the government and the board of transport commissioners to proceed with the operation of the pipe line, it will have wide powers of expropriation which should never, under any circumstances, be given to unknown people, for an unknown destination, and over an unknown route. I cannot think of anything which would indicate less regard for the responsibility of members of parliament than to give such wide and sweeping powers with no rigid definition of the route this pipe line would follow.
On a number of occasions when other pipe lines have been dealt with we have learned that these companies are quite ready to change the route, depending on what they think is most likely to meet with approval. They have the power to change the route. We are therefore asked, with all the responsibility and the authority of parliament, to confer these
3522	HOUSE OF
Boundary Pipeline Corporation sweeping powers upon unknown people who acquire their rights under a charter issued in this way.
On an earlier occasion, some two years ago, I suggested a procedure which would be in keeping with the ordinary practices in matters of this kind and which would take away from the House of Commons and the Senate the pretence of exercising judgment with regard to something about which we have not sufficient evidence to exercise proper judgment. The procedure to which I refer would be simple. It would be for the government to introduce a simple amendment to the Pipe Lines Act. It need be only a single section which would say that the kind of company described in the Pipe Lines Act and which would obtain the powers conferred by the Pipe Lines Act would be a company which obtained an ordinary charter under the dominion Companies Act. It might be suggested by someone that this would be exercising still less control over the incorporation of companies of this nature. I should like to see no pretence whatever that real control is exercised. It is true that this debate has provided an opportunity to place before the committee arguments in support of a policy of Canadian priority in relation to the use of our resources. I submit that such a policy can be expressed, and established in some other way. I submit that a policy could be declared by a resolution, and that such a policy would guide those who are called upon to exercise their discretion in permitting these pipe line companies to carry on business. We do not yet know whether this company would be allowed to carry on business if it did get a charter. For that reason, amongst others, I do not think we should be granting a charter, which has some real money value the moment it is granted by this house, when we have no way of knowing whether or not that charter is ever going to give anyone the right to proceed.
I hope the time that has been occupied in discussing ihis subject for the purpose of indicating that a very substantial number of members do not want to see charters granted in this way will impress upon the government the desirability of such an amendment. That does not mean that a company which obtains a charter under the dominion Companies Act can proceed with a pipe line simply by virtue of the charter. It means that a company which obtains a charter in that way will then require to obtain permission to proceed with the operation of a pipe line by an application to the board of transport commissioners. It still must obtain permission from the government of Alberta if the gas or oil comes from


the soil of Alberta. It must also obtain permission from the dominion government, and therefore the granting of a charter under the Companies Act would still leave the matter for decision by those authorities who now have no opportunity to exercise any real judgment as to whether or not the applicant in question should have the right to carry on business.
We would save time, and there would be no pretence about parliament having passed judgment. In that case any number of people who wanted to get charters could get them; and each would meet fairly before the board of transport commissioners and before the governments concerned and be able to present evidence in the ordinary way. No one would be left out in the cold. Anybody who was prepared to pay for a charter could get that charter, and the whole question would then be one for a semi-judicial body, the board of transport commissioners, to decide, with subsequent decisions by the dominion and provincial governments concerned. That, it seems to me, is a sensible, businesslike procedure which is in keeping with the general practices in regard to matters of this kind. It is one which would take away from parliament something that is occupying a great deal of time unnecessarily, and which I am sure will continue to occupy a great deal of time unnecessarily if this procedure is still followed.
I made that proposal before; in fact I made it on March 20, 1950. I hope that now, in 1952, the government may decide that this would be a better way of proceeding. If on the other hand the government has some other alternative, I certainly would be very happy to support any method which would take away from the parliament of Canada the pretence of passing judgment upon something in regard to which we are not furnished adequate information.
There is another point in regard to this matter that I should like to discuss. I should like to discuss the merits of this particular application and indicate why I think it is desirable that there be some clearly declared policy in regard to matters of this kind. This particular application is for a charter to construct and operate a gas pipe line from the province of Alberta into the province of Manitoba; and it is disclosed by those who have argued in support of the measure that the pipe line will then proceed into the .United States.
May I emphasize once again that I for one ; im not arguing against the export to the Jnited States in sensible and reasonable [uantities of any raw material or commodity produced in this country. Nevertheless I

do believe that the first concern of the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada should be the advancement of Canada and the employment of our own resources to the greatest possible advantage of our own people. Just a few days ago I presented an argument in this house in regard to wider employment of some of our raw materials in Canada. I was interested and somewhat surprised to find that argument summarized in the opinion of some people, as an argument in support of a ban on export. Hansard will disclose that I suggested no such thing; that I suggested the very contrary. I am saying that now simply to emphasize that whatever argument I am putting forward, it is not an argument in regard to a ban on this or any other raw material or natural resource that we possess, where it is in our interest that we export it. What I am saying is that the course we adopt should assure that we shall gain the greatest possible advantage from our own resources here in Canada. With that thought in mind let us see what the situation actually is.
Both Ontario and Quebec through their governments have indicated their desire to have natural gas from the province of Alberta. That has been stated without any reservations by members of the governments of these two provinces. Arguments that were put forth in support of this measure in no way dispose of the argument that was presented on the other side, that if this particular charter were granted it would for the time being prevent the construction of another pipe line to carry natural gas to the east. Therefore one of the questions to be decided as a matter of principle is whether or not this House of Commons, if it is called upon to exercise some measure of judgment, is or is not going to say that it concurs in the representations made by these provincial governments and is willing to take a course which will assure the transmission of natural gas for use in these two provinces.
Ontario already is using a very substantial amount of natural gas coming into the province from the United States. For that very reason it would be unreasonable to suggest that we should not be prepared to co-operate at different points in Canada where that co-operation seems reasonable. I think it would be very reasonable for the government of Canada to discuss with the government of the United States appropriate exchanges of natural gas at different points along the border.
The Canadian government knows that at this time there is an application before the appropriate authority in Washington to permit the export of natural gas into Ontario, a
Boundary Pipeline Corporation province which has been using natural gas from the United States for some time. Actually there is a contract now in existence under which gas is transmitted from the Texas panhandle up to Ontario; and that contract calls for the delivery of more than five billion cubic feet of natural gas a year. That however has not yet been formally approved by the authority in Washington which deals with matters of this kind. Therefore the whole situation in regard to that export is in a state of uncertainty.
I think this is the very kind of thing that could be dealt with properly by discussions between the two governments. Where there is any possibility of export, in a case of this kind, it should be as the result of negotiation and arrangement of that nature rather than by a hit or miss process such as that indicated in the measure now before us.
If a pipe line should carry natural gas through to Ontario and Quebec, that would not mean Ontario would be denied any natural gas for which it might have contracted with the United States. It would simply mean that the very much larger quantities that are required than those they can hope to obtain from the United States would become available right across the great industrial areas of northern and eastern Ontario. Also it would mean that this gas would become available in the busy industrial centres of Quebec.
Still, if that were a large pipe line, export at different points might be arranged by consultation between the governments of Canada and the United States. But if we are going to deal with this on its merits, then I submit that the first pipe line to the east which should be approved is a pipe line that carries its gas into the large industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec so as to assure to these provinces this natural resource which will help so much to develop the whole country.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: What about Bruce?

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
I was under the impression that Bruce is still in Ontario, and I hope it will continue to remain in Ontario. I had not heard that it had declared its independence at any time. But I would certainly hope that the fine county of Bruce, along with all the other counties in Ontario and Quebec, would benefit from the available supply of this cheap and very efficient fuel.
I have heard the comment during this debate that this is an argument in favour of Ontario and Quebec. I have heard it said that it does not very much benefit the intervening provinces in western Canada, nor does it greatly benefit the maritime provinces. Well, we cannot change geography,

Boundary Pipeline Corporation much though we might like at times to do so. We cannot change the fact that there would still be a very long pipe line to the maritime provinces, if it were to be carried down there.
Nevertheless the area within which gas can be transmitted economically is increasing all the time, and it is conceivable that at some time even that might happen. I should be more inclined to hope that some time in the not too distant future the liquefaction of coal, or other employments of coal in the maritime provinces, might give them the advantage of their own raw materials which are in such abundance in those provinces in a form that could be changed into another type of fuel, and then into either gas or electricity. However, that is something for the future, something to consider at another time.
So far as this measure is concerned, I do submit we should not overlook the fact that the very large population of Ontario and Quebec provides a sound commercial outlet for the natural gas from Alberta. It has been noticeable that during the course of these discussions members of this house from Alberta have concurred in that suggestion. They have indicated their own opinion that this pipe line is not a sound proposition, and that if we are going to be called upon to deal with matters of this kind in the House of Commons, then the charters to be granted should have the interests of Canada as their first consideration.
I would hope also that we would bear in mind that when we strengthen the productive capacity of any one part of Canada, we strengthen the whole economy of Canada and increase the possibility that this country as a whole may advance, and that there may be an improvement in the situation in every part of the country.
With that thought in mind I would hope that in some way independently of this measure a clearly stated policy would be adopted by the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada under which, in the employment of our resources, we would place the interests of Canada and its people first, while at all times expressing our willingness to export resources on a reasonable basis so long as we do not limit our own opportunity for expansion and growth by so doing.
When I began these remarks I left no doubt that I was not making my argument in the expectation that it would change the opinion of those who have presented the measure to the house. I do hope that the absurdity of wasting so much time to prevent the

adoption of an unwise measure will impress upon the government the wisdom of following some other course in dealing with applications of this nature.
I would hope that when this session comes to an end-and I certainly hope this bill has not been passed at that time-the government might decide that before we meet again there will be some provision for the issuing of a charter in a simple manner, and a procedure which would place anyone wishing to obtain a charter on an equal basis when appearing before the board of transport commissioners and the governments affected. They would then make the decision as to who is going to have the right to build and operate a pipe line. I will go further and say that instead of continuing this debate for the remainder of this session-I say this in all earnestness-the government should consider introducing a simple amendment to the Pipe Lines Act along the lines I have advocated. It could be a brief amendment adding a section providing that a company referred to in the act shall be a company with a charter obtained under the dominion Companies Act. I am reasonably sure that the members of this house would support such an amendment. It would take much less time to deal with that very effective amendment than will be wasted if this bill is brought up for discussion once again.

The suggestion is that it is all wrong for members of the House of Commons to examine the provisions of these bills, that the Pipe Lines Act should be changed so that any company incorporated under the Companies Act would have these rights. We all know that all that is necessary to be incorporated under the Companies Act is to

file the necessary documents with the Secretary of State, pay the necessary fee, and then the incorporators would have everything they are asking this parliament to give them, by this bill.
Why not do that? That procedure has been considered. The reason was referred to by the leader of the opposition. Incorporation under the Pipe Lines Act carries with it the right of expropriation. It has been the practice of this parliament since confederation to be very jealous of granting incorporations that carry with them the right of expropriation.
Hon. members are aware that anyone wishing a charter to build a railroad or lay track for a distance of more than seven miles must come to this parliament with a private bill. Why? Because by the terms of the Transport Act the authority for laying of that track carries with it the right of expropriation. Anyone who wishes to build a bridge across international waters must come to this parliament to be incorporated because he is asking for rights over international waters, which rights are very jealously guarded by parliament.
I quite agree with the hon. leader that any reputable company that is properly financed, that is composed of reputable people and that has an objective that is reasonably sound should be able to obtain incorporation by a private bill approved by this House of Commons. That has always been my contention. I ask hon. members to remember that all this bill gives is incorporation; it does not grant any rights whatever to the company except the right which the leader of the opposition says should be granted as a matter of course under the Companies Act.
I do not agree that anyone should be able to go to the Secretary of State and by virtue of the fact that he files certain documents obtain an incorporation as a pipe line company when such incorporation may lead to obtaining the power of expropriation. It has always been the belief of the government that anyone who wants the right of eminent domain, the right of expropriation, should be compelled to come to parliament where he can be examined by members of parliament or by anyone who has a particular interest in the incorporation. The member representing that particular district should have the right to ask the incorporators any question he wishes to ask and obtain a satisfactory answer.
I believe that is a desirable safeguard. The incorporators of pipe line companies should be compelled to appear before a committee of parliament, to show what their interests are, to indicate their intentions, to prove {heir
Boundary Pipeline Corporation financial bona fides and, in short, to establish themselves as a reputable company.
You say, "That is perfectly reasonable. We pass several private bills of that type every session." We have run into two long filibusters in connection with pipe lines. One bill was before this parliament for two sessions before it was finally passed. That was the second bill. It is said that there is something wrong about this bill, but it is exactly like a bill which gave the same privileges and set out the same purposes of incorporation, which was passed at a previous session. That bill had to do with a pipe line from Alberta to Winnipeg and then southward, and there was no difficulty about it. But in connection with this bill we have had this blockade lasting for several months.
I do not want to impute motives, but it seems to me that this opposition is really not opposition to a bill. There is nothing wrong with the proposed incorporation, as the leader of the opposition admits. This is opposition in favour of an incorporation which was granted previously. That was obviously the case two years ago, admittedly so. At that time it was contended that there was a perfectly good Canadian company that had been incorporated to build a pipe line from Alberta westward and then down across the international border, so why incorporate another company that would be a competitor.

Mr. Chairman, though not a
member of the official opposition I feel there are two or three things I should like to say with respect to the bill now before us. Certainly no one can accuse me of having participated in a filibuster, because I have not taken any time in the house previously in connection with this matter or any other comparable measure which has come before


us. I was particularly interested in the observations made by the leader of the opposition during the concluding portion of his remarks. He referred to the absence of a national policy with respect to the question of gas export. My personal conviction is that in the absence of such a national policy, clear cut and definitely defined, we have encountered the difficulties which are before us now and have been before us during the weeks and months that have gone by.
A moment ago the minister indicated that when a company desiring incorporation appears before a committee of the house every member is provided with an opportunity to secure definite information with respect to the specific route and to raise whatever objections he may desire to raise. I take exception to that statement. I am not aware of the fact that this company filed a specific proposal as to route.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext: On a question of privilege, if the hon. member will let me explain, I did not say that. All a company comes to this house for is the purpose of incorporation. The matter of the route is a question for the board of transport commissioners.

subtopic: BOUNDARY PIPELINE CORPORATION
speechtext:
That is true, but did not the minister assert that when such a company appeared before the committee of the house members were afforded an opportunity to raise objections to any such specific acts of expropriation, let us say, which may affect the particular districts they represent? Certainly my experience leads me to the conclusion that no such opportunity is actually afforded at all. When a company appears before a committee of the house it is for the express purpose of putting before the committee a general idea of what the company proposes to do with respect to export, and information relative to the method of financing the company's operations. Beyond that I am very much afraid that members of the committee are left pretty much in the dark.
My fundamental interest in this matter at the present time stems from the fact that when the master pipe line measure was being considered by a committee of the other place the attorney general of my province appeared before that committee and pleaded with them to lay down regulations which would make it necessary for a company of this kind to appear before a semi-judicial body for the purpose of securing the right to incorporate under the Companies Act. Mr. Maynard, the attorney general of Alberta, in anticipation of some of the very difficulties we have encountered since that time, pleaded with

the committee to give favourable consideration to his proposal. I well recall the reception his proposal met before that committee, because I witnessed it. It was turned down. To my mind so much of the difficulty we have encountered since that time stems from that very fact.
So far as safeguards in connection with expropriation are concerned, certainly the board of transport commissioners could take every precaution to determine whether the company applying for incorporation was complying with all the regulations with respect to expropriation or anything else, as a matter of fact, covered by any legislation existing in Canada today. I agree with those who have laid down the principle that, so far as the export of gas from one part of Canada to another part and thence elsewhere is concerned, we should give prime consideration to the requirements of our own country first. I am not one of those who assert that that involves the piping of gas from Alberta to the maritimes or, as a matter of fact, even to the province of Quebec or conceivably even to the province of Ontario, because I recognize that there is merit in a policy whereby we might exchange gas with our United States friends to the south.
Certainly we have to approach the matter from the economic point of view when making a decision in that respect. I think my own province is quite justified in the position it has taken with respect to meeting its own requirements first, and certainly I believe the rest of us are justified in asserting that we should see to it that the requirements of the Canadian people are met as far as possible. With respect to the bill now before us, I have no particular interest in the persons involved but I suggest it is unfortunate that we followed the course of action which we adopted in 1949 because it led to this difficulty. I think even now it is not [DOT]too late for the government to introduce amendments to the master pipe line legislation which would enable us to refer these applications to a semi-judicial body-I have already mentioned the board of transport commissioners-for the purpose of dealing with them instead of doing it in the House of Commons. I feel confident that just as long as we have applications of this kind *coming before the house, just so long are we going to encounter the type of debate we have had during the past several weeks and months. When dealing with the question of committee reports, I understood the hon. member to say that only the members who were on the committee read the reports; the others did not read them. It is the other way round. It is the members who are not on the committees who, in my opinion, need the reports.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The hon. member said "need" not "read".

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I always read the reports to see what the hon. member for St. John's West has said on any question. If I did not read the reports I would not know.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I cannot return the compliment.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have to look after whatever parliament gives us to translate. It is not our business to say what we should do. We do what we are told by parliament, and the additional men we engage during rush periods are in the nature of a temporary staff, as it were. They are paid for doing their work and we think we save money because we do not have them on the staff all the year round.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The Secretary of State said that when the house was sitting they needed additional translators or additional staff. I should like to know what the translating staff have to do when the house is not sitting.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have to translate reports and correspondence from all departments of government throughout the year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Do the interpreters who interpret in regard to censorship of books for the Minister of National Revenue come under the jurisdiction of that minister, or under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member; I do not think the minister heard the question.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I did not hear the question, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
There are certain interpreters used in the department that censors books and literature. That censorship is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue. My question was whether the interpreters under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State are used for that purpose,

or whether these interpreters are under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue, who is supposed to be the censor of literature in Canada.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have nothing to do with interpreters. If any document has to be translated for any department of the government our bureau for translations does it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: With the exception of the Senate, because the Senate has kept its jurisdiction over the translators and has set a good example to the House of Commons. In 1934 the House of Commons abandoned its rights over the translators, while the Senate kept them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Temiscouata will not mind at this point if a part of what he said when he was on his feet before is corrected. He was correct, I would say, in telling us that the translators do not come under the jurisdiction of the House of Commons, but the other groups to whom he referred before, the reporters, the postal branch, the stenographic branch and so on, all come under the jurisdiction of the Speaker. They are listed under legislation.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Not for their appointment, as it did before. That is what I am talking about.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is not what the hon. member said.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Oh, yes. I used the English language. My hon. friend is quick enough to understand it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It seems to me there is still a difference between two authorities, and I should like to have this matter straightened out. As I understood him, the hon. member for Temiscouata told us that we no longer have any control over the translators. On the other hand, the Secretary of State, as I understood him, said the translators did what the House of Commons ordered them to do. These two statements, if I correctly summarized them, seem to me to be in conflict.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We do the work that is sent to us to do.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: A service department.

437.	Canada Temperance Act, $1,000.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Can the Secretary of State explain why this item of $1,000 for legal fees with respect to the Canada Temperance Act is necessary?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
That item is there in connection with the Canada Temperance Act to be used if necessary in places where the
Supply-Secretary of State federal government has to foot the bill. I do not know whether anything will arise this year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What are these places? I am seeking information about this?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This act is now in force in only two places for which we have any responsibility. Should it be put in force in some other part of the country where we have responsibility we may have to use that vote.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does the Secretary of State not think that we could wait until we put the act in force in these places where we have responsibility before asking parliament for this money, which is the basis for taxation which is struck?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No; we must have the vote there, because we do not know when the occasion is going to arise.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: How long is it since an occasion has arisen?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Any place in Canada can put the act in force. If that should happen it may be that we shall incur expenses in connection with it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am sorry; I do not quite see the force of the minister's explanation. It would seem to me that if this is an act which it may become the responsibility of this government to enforce-the Secretary of State has not yet said how long it is since that situation has arisen, but I would gather that it is many years-surely the Department of Justice could make counsel available to his department to look after it. Surely the Department of Justice and the counsel available within that department could look after it. I must say that at the present time I cannot see why this item of $1,000 should be included for something that looks like a contingency which never arises.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This is a federal act. I understand that in Ontario the province bears the cost of enforcement wherever it may be necessary. However, there are parts of Canada where this is not done. Should the act be put into force in one of those places where the province will not bear the expense, then we have to do it. That is the reason for the vote.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Will the minister tell us how long it is since that situation has arisen? How long is it since the act has been put into force in any place where this government would have jurisdiction?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Until 1950 the act was in force in the county of Beauce, in the province of Quebec.

Supply-Secretary of State

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I take it that it is not in force there now, and that there has been no need for this money in the last two years.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is it not the minister's opinion that we should dispense with the item until we have notice that the act has been proclaimed elsewhere?

speechtext: We cannot wait until the next session. If it happens to come into force in the meantime we have to enforce it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This has been going on for years. How much is in the fund now?

439. Patent division (including the former patent record division), $840,391.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I notice there is an increase in staff from 13 to 22 in the administration division, and that in the patent division there is an increase in number of staff from 138 to 146. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have here the report of the commissioner of patents for the year ended March 31, 1951. There are one or two things in it with which I am not familiar. What does the London accord cover, and do we come in under it?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Immediately after the war the London accord became an arrangement
[Mr. Bradley.)



under which citizens of allied countries could get, royalty free, the right to use wholly-owned German patents.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is a very brief and, I suppose, complete explanation. But I see on page 5 a reference to 11,000 claims under the international convention. Would the minister explain the significance of the international convention as distinct from the London accord?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Under the Paris convention some 50 or 60 countries by agreement among themselves made an arrangement whereby nationals of those several countries would have the same rights in other countries, in respect of industrial property, as in the country of origin.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Would the minister enumerate those who are included? Perhaps it would be easier to enumerate those who are not included.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: And would the minister please explain his answer? It is not very clear to us.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Roughly, in the western world it would include Canada, the United States, Mexico and Brazil. It includes also the western European countries. Roughly speaking, other countries would be out.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister has referred to 50 or 60 countries, and in enumerating them he referred to Canada, the United States, Brazil and European countries. That would be only about a dozen. Is South America out?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have not the figures here at the moment, but if my hon. friend wishes to have them I can get them for him accurately.

Item agreed to.
440. Copyright and industrial designs division, including a contribution of $2,100 to the union office for the protection of literary and artistic works, $20,279.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Earlier this session I had occasion to bring to the attention of the minister a suggestion made by the exhibition association in Vancouver that at agricultural fairs where musical compositions are played, not for profit but simply for the entertainment of the crowds attending such fairs, they should be exempt from the payment of copyright fees on such musical works. Such musical pieces are played not for profit but for the entertainment of the people attending the fair, and it is contended that they should be exempt from the payment of the copyright fees on musical works.
I understand that attempts have been made several times in the past to frame a section

for the Copyright Act which would l;ave the effect of exempting agricultural fairs from the payment of royalties on music played under such conditions. Apparently those attempts were not successful, and I wonder if the minister would say what is the position today and what is the government's attitude toward the request of the Vancouver organization-they may have been joined by others-that the legislation should be amended to exempt agricultural fairs from the payment of royalties on the performance of copyrighted music.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I understand that this matter has been referred to the supreme court and apparently their views are not particularly favourable to the organization my hon. friend has mentioned. We are prepared to take this matter under consideration, but just what will be the result from the standpoint of policy I am not prepared to say at the moment. I understand there are cogent arguments which could be used against it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Did the minister say that the supreme court does not look with favour on the organization to which I have referred?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The Supreme Court of Canada gave a judgment, the interpretation of which was unfavourable.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Perhaps I could put it this way: the supreme court gave a judgment which interpreted the Copyright Act in a sense which was unfavourable to the organization.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That was some time ago and I understand that representations have since been made that this action be taken. I have received letters and I have written to the minister about it. I wonder if he could indicate what is the present position.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The position is unchanged but, as I said before, we are prepared to consider that particular point when we revise the act.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: When will the revision of the act be undertaken?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Probably within the next twelve months.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The total vote is $20,279, and over 20 per cent of that is for stationery. That seems completely out of line with the other items. They must be great letter writers.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There are a lot of copyright certificates to issue, and copies have to be issued as well.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Has the department given any consideration to a problem which arises in connection with the importation of educational
55704-223J
Supply-Secretary of State and scientific books. I understand that books of that type come in duty free, but because of the provisions of our Copyright Act the Canadian purchaser of such books may not get the benefit. The Copyright Act permits the publisher of such a book to send these books to a Canadian agent and set whatever price he desires on them. I have had complaints from people in Vancouver that they have had to pay several dollars more for a book in Canada than it was selling for in the United States.
One man wrote to the United States for a book listed at a certain price but the publisher told him that he must get it from the Canadian agent, and he found several dollars was added arbitrarily to the United States price. In other words the copyright law is being used to extort higher prices from Canadian purchasers of these books, and that seems to me to be unreasonable.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am not prepared to give the hon. member an answer right now, but we will look into it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is most unfair that such a situation should be created by our copyright law which apparently gives such wide protection to the holder of a copyright that he in turn can hold up the public and deprive them of the benefit that should accrue from no duty being payable. I ask the minister to look into the whole situation.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I shall be glad to do so.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What is this contribution to the union office for the protection of literary and artistic works? Why do we have to contribute to this union?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We are members of the organization and we have to contribute to its upkeep.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What is that?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The Berne union.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wrote to the minister about a year ago stating that representations had been made to me that an amendment should be made to the act so that horticultural creations could be patented or copyrighted. Could the Secretary of State say what action has been taken? It seemed to me that the larger horticulturists were anxious to have this amendment, whereas it might prove detrimental to the smaller growers who would have great difficulty in paying for the necessary copyright for patents or whatever it is called.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
This comes under patents, but I have no objection to answering. The matter is under consideration now. I believe a system of protection has been introduced in the

Supply-Secretary of State United States, and we are watching to see how they get along with it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Will you keep in mind the interests of the small growers?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is so easy for a big firm to import a creation and get a copyright on it or a patent, as we call it, whereas the smaller man who has developed a floral creation cannot get a copyright. Therefore his interest is excluded from the development of that particular species. I do not think it is altogether a good thing to have this copyright included unless adequate safeguards are given.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: With respect to this union office, is the government a member of the union and what union is it?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is a union for the protection of industrial property.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It says literary and artistic works in the book of estimates.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speechtext: Then as I understand it this is an international union of various nations. What do they do? Are they joined together to give mutual protection?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
