subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I think I know the cause of the levity, but I regard the matter to which I have drawn attention as quite serious. It seems to me that somebody has made a slip. The paragraph reads:
When vacancies occur, a sincere and planned effort is made to select the best person available, regardless of sex, religion, nationality, political belief, personal sponsorship, overseas service or any other extraneous consideration.
I agree that, in civil service matters, all those considerations except the last one might properly be designated as extraneous. Surely the civil service commission does not regard overseas service as an extraneous consideration.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would tell us whether that applies to appointments or promotions?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: According to the book it appears, as I said before when I read this the first time, Mr. Chairman, under the general heading of "Your promotion opportunities".

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I understand that overseas service does not apply to promotions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does the Secretary of State feel that even if that is the case it is proper to refer to overseas service as an extraneous consideration.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
From the standpoint of
promotions it is apparently not to be considered; that is what the statement says.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We shall leave it to the Secretary of State to get a copy of this booklet, and see what he really thinks about it. May I ask the minister whether he has any up-to-date figures as to the number of civil servants in the various categories, permanent, temporary permanent, temporary and any other category. I do not want to confuse him-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Take permanents first.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We shall take the permanents first, then the temporary-permanent and temporary. Can the minister give the figures for this year, last year and perhaps the year before that?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There are, roughly, 130,000 employees under the civil service commission. Of those 60,000 are permanent and 70,000 are temporary.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What was the situation a year ago and two years ago?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The increase in the permanents last year was 10,000 and the year before about 6,000, so the number of temporary employees would be reduced accordingly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Can the Secretary of State divide the temporaries into ordinary temporaries and temporary permanents?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have no such distinction.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I should like to bring to the attention of the Secretary of State a case which concerns pensions of civil servants. Apparently some distinction is made between veterans who served in the first world war and those who served in the second world war.
A veteran of world war I entering the civil service after July, 1924, can have his war service counted towards his superannuation on paying double the normal contribution for that periods-that is, the employee's share and the government's share-plus 4 per cent interest.
However, as he entered the service after July, 1924, he comes under the provisions of part I of the Civil Service Act which stipulates a ten-year salary average to establish his rate of pension.
Had he entered the service prior to July, 1924, part IV of the act would have applied and his pension would have been based on the average salary of five years. In short, the 1914-18 veteran, although he is purchasing service for that period at a high rate plus interest, is denied the privilege of being

placed under part IV with resulting benefits in retirement.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think that is a matter for the Department of Finance, not for this department.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does not the question of civil service pensions come under this item?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does not the civil service commission set the rules of entry?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: May I ask whether the civil service commission has anything to do with the prospect of the five-day week, or is that matter also to be referred to the Minister of Finance?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: All right. We will take that matter up with the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There is just one other question I want to ask and it is this. Under what rules does a person become permanent? Who sets the designation? I have in mind one case of a civil servant who has had 27 years with one department, has been promoted three or four times, and has been actually in charge of one of the subdepartments of this department in the absence of the director. Yet despite all efforts, and despite 27 years of continuous service, he has not been able to be classed as a permanent civil servant. A great deal of that service, in fact most of it, was given overseas. This civil servant is in the department of immigration, as a matter of fact. That fact may have something to do with the matter. After that length of service it would seem to me a gross injustice not to have that civil servant classed as a permanent civil servant, particularly having regard to the fact that he has for years requested ' that he be considered as such. Who decides? Is it the minister? Is it the director? Is it the civil service commission? Who makes the decision?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The decision will depend upon two questions. The first is whether the work he is doing is of a permanent character. Second, the department must report that his work is satisfactory and ask for his transfer to the permanent list.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The work is of a permanent character.
Supply-Secretary of State

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would be good enough to give me the details of that particular case. I will be glad to look into it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I will, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does the civil service commission make any appointments? .

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I understand that it made
29,000	appointments last year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Did it make those appointments on the record of the candidates, having regard to how they are appraised on their examinations?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is so; yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Or did it merely make recommendations to the government instead of making the appointments?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: How many civil servants are ordinarily resident in Ottawa?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: About 32,000.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is a high number for this city. I take it that the people of other provinces and other cities outside of Ottawa are given opportunities to take examinations for appointment here? Would that be correct?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Following up that question there is one other I wish to ask. As to the people at the extremities of the country-for instance, those in British Columbia or in Newfoundland-does it work out in practice that although they are notified of positions, they do not actually enter to any extent and compete?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The commission has regional offices in every province in Canada, I understand, and they issue notices. Application can be made through the regional office in each province.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Are there actually many applications for appointments that are being made here in Ottawa?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: As a matter of actual fact quite a large proportion of officials do come from the extremities of Canada, but frankly not as many as we would like.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The minister just said the commission had made 29,000 appointments, I think it was, last year. If I remember correctly he said earlier that the increase in the number of civil servants had been only 10 per cent of the total.

Supply-Secretary of State

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: He said the number of permanents had increased by 10,000 and that the number of temporaries had decreased by the same number.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What does that indicate as to wastage? The argument is apparently stronger if there are 29,000 appointments made and the numbers are no greater.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The 29,000 includes wastage. The actual increase was about 8,000.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is the point I want to get at. Is there wastage of 21,000?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is turnover.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That seems terrific. Is there anything that can be said in mitigation of what seems to be a rather astonishing figure?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It has been much higher during the last two years. For that we blame the industrial situation to some extent.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does the minister mean that the members of the service are able to get so much better salaries outside that they are leaving the service?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: In a good many cases that is so; yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Then the turnover in the civil service is of the nature of 24 per cent per annum.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I have not worked out the percentage.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There are 130,000 civil servants. Is the turnover 29,000?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have to take into account the fact that a good many of those appointments are for short terms, and there may be a turnover in one appointment perhaps two or three times a year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Are most of these 29,000 in the lower brackets, or are a fair percentage of them in the upper brackets? What I am interested in is not only the turnover in the lower brackets, but the appeal by industry for the higher paid civil servants. Are we losing a great number of civil servants in the higher brackets to industry, and particularly civil servants who have technical skills?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The minister said a few moments ago the government does not interfere in connection with appointments. I understand examinations are held for appointments. After the examination a person
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).)

is appointed. Those who rate in order of merit are listed, I understand. Has it been the experience during the past year that all those who happen to be in second place have received the appointment, if a vacancy occurred in the position?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No; there are cases in which the department rejects the higher candidate.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What happens in that case? Is there a report to the minister? I have known of a case where I think that happened. What happens in such an incident as that? Does it remain wholly with the commission or not, where the commission decides not to act according to the strict principles laid down. I am not saying that is never the right thing to do, but I am asking whether in such a case there is any report to the minister of the circumstances. Is there a check of any kind on the commission in the matter?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to a rejection by the department?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I understood the minister to say there were certain cases where the person who came highest, according to the ordinary test, was not appointed. I know that happens occasionally and I am asking the minister whether in such a case there is any procedure whereby a report is made to the minister or to someone else. In other words, in such an exceptional case is there some reviewing authority?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
So far as the commission is concerned the candidate who gets the highest marks gets the job, but he may be rejected by the department. Section 24 of the act reads as follows:
The deputy head may, at any time before the expiration of six months, reject any person assigned or appointed to any position under his control or direction, or he may extend the period of probation within which such person may be rejected for another six months: and the cause of rejection, or the reason for extending the period of probation, shall be reported by the deputy head to the commission.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
That is the
other way around.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That is to say, the deputy head may for cause refuse to continue an appointment and then refer it to the commission?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
That part is clear; but does the minister now say that the commission is bound, absolutely bound,

to appoint the person who receives the highest marks? "Marks" was the word he used. Is it as definite and as rigid as that? That surprises me. I am also wondering if it is quite as rigid as that in practice.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I do not think I shall read the section unless the hon. member requires it, but ordinarily the decision is that the person getting the highest number of marks gets the position, so far as the civil service commission is concerned, but considerations may arise occasionally which would cause them to give a different decision.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What would those considerations be?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Special qualifications.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: That comes back to this.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I will read the section of the act to you, if you like.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Let me put
my question first. A few minutes ago the minister .used the word "marks" which suggested that the whole thing depended on examination. Now he is using a broader term, which I think might be quite sensible, an additional test. But I want to know whether in fact it is marks, or whether the commission is entitled to use its discretion. For instance, there are certain appointments that are made partly as a result of written examinations and partly as a result of a personal interview. What is the situation here?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The section reads:
The commission shall thereupon appoint the person whose name stands highest upon the commission's list of eligible persons for the class in which the position is found and who is willing to accept the appointment; in case there is no such list for the class, the commission shall forthwith hold an examination and, if necessary to prevent any serious interference with the public business, but not otherwise, may fill the position at once by making a temporary appointment as prescribed herein.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am getting more confused every moment because that seems to refer to a list. If that list was not available and you went on and had an examination, what would happen? Would the minister read those words again?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
They read:
The commission shall thereupon appoint the person whose name stands highest upon the commission's list of eligible persons-

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: How is that list arrived at?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
By a competitive examination. An examination may be either written or oral or both oral and written.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I want to return to the item which was up a moment ago, namely the item of wastage. The minister seemed to give the answer in a very general and somewhat offhand way. All we got in the end was that the wastage was predominantly among the junior ranks, which is what one would expect because there are more of them. But I would have thought that would be a matter of such deep concern to the minister and to his senior officials that we should be able to get some rather detailed information. I would have thought there must be some rather significant facts which should enter in here. I do not feel like leaving it in that entirely general, and if I may say so, offhand way.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I understand this subject is being considered very seriously by the commission now.

speechtext:
Does the civil service commission make appointments? I asked that question before, and the answer was that it does. However, a little over a year ago I was interested in two individuals who had taken part in an examination. Altogether there were four or five who took the examination for a civil service position, but the man who ranked highest in both the written and oral tests did not get the appointment. The man who came third was appointed. Of course, according to my belief, the civil service commission did not make any appointment at all; I always think it is the government that makes the appointment. Of course I may be wrong in that.
In this instance, according to the regulations of the commission the man at the top should have received the appointment. I do not wish to give names because the man who was appointed is a good chap and a friend of mine, but his capabilities are not nearly equal to those of the man who was first in the test. They are not in the same class at all.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Perhaps he got it because he was a friend of yours.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: No; the fellow who got the job was a strong Liberal.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: And that is why he was a friend of yours?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: He was a friend of mine, just the same.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We make allowances.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
And that was the reason he got the job. It is a pity to have this question bandied about here tonight. What we should do is to have the officers of the civil service commission before us for an hour or two so we could iron out some things we all know

Supply-Secretary of State are not as smooth or as straight as they should be. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wish to repeat that the government does not interfere with appointments made by the civil service commission. There are cases when departments reject those who have been selected by the commission, but they would constitute less than one per cent of the whole.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wish to say only a few words, and they are words of congratulations to the civil service commission upon the very fine job they are doing. I say that seriously and sincerely. My only complaint in the county of Charlotte is that those who receive the appointments are all Tories. I repeat that in my view the commission is doing a fine job, and they are to be congratulated upon the way they make appointments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Have you never seen D. R. Bishop?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What is the procedure when a minister requires a certain man? Can he appoint him without going through the civil service commission? The Department of Defence Production would be a case in point. The minister of that department might require a certain man for a specific job. Generally the man selected must sacrifice a great deal when he accepts the job. However, the minister wants one man he knows could fill that job, and he does not want to go through the civil service commission. The man is needed in a hurry. What is the machinery? Is it possible to by-pass the civil service commission in a case of that kind?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It can be done where parliament gives authority to do so; but not otherwise.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Parliament gives authority through what means? Is it by order in council?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: By statute.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: With regard to the returned soldier preference, is there a point where that preference does not operate as against nonsoldiers?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If a returned veteran comes up to the standard required by the department, he has absolute preference over all other candidates.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is that only in respect of appointments?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: For appointments, yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Does that mean that the man who was able to pass the examination would not receive the appointment, but that a returned soldier would? How does that effect the department concerned?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: So far as we know the preference given to veterans has not done any serious harm to the service.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Is special consideration given to a soldier who has enlisted in the Canadian army but who, because of his officer holding him in some special job, has been prevented from going overseas?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: There is no provision for them now.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Would the minister take that into consideration?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I would ask the minister to make a statement concerning competitive examinations held to fill positions that become vacant during the year. Would he indicate the number of examinations set, the cost of setting them, the number of candidates, and the cost of conducting examinations.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: We have not those figures at hand now. To secure them would involve some research, but if the hon. member wishes to have them I can get them for him.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The minister said there was a wastage of about 29,000 per year. That would seem to be important, and perhaps the process of filling positions that become vacant would be costly. The information I have asked would be helpful.

speechtext: What is the cost of recruitment for the civil service? The breakdown refers chiefly to the salaries of personnel including clerks, investigators, organizers and the like. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: In previous years there was a list at the end of the civil service commission report indicating those who served on the civil service commission board. speechtext: The list is available to the hon. member if he wants it. It was deleted from the report purely as a matter of cutting costs.

speechtext: I would like everybody to benefit from it.

speechtext: How many appointments to the public service-do not let us call it the civil service-are made without the tests which have been described to us having to be passed? speechtext: Yes, if the positions are under the jurisdiction of the commission.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
The two votes having to do with this branch show a decrease of $1,279, and I am rather sorry to see that tendency although I am all in favour of economy. I think at the present time the archives is one branch of the government service which actually requires more funds to do its necessary work. I rise as one who is interested in the archives to express my appreciation- I am sure I am joined in this by a lot of other people-of the excellent work being done by the dominion archivist and his staff. We are fortunate in our present dominion archivist because of his wide knowledge and ability, his academic training and his great interest in the archives of Canada. I am sure that everyone will agree that anyone wishing to secure anything from the archives is met with the most courteous and efficient service on the part of the archivist and his staff.
I think the present report on the public archives is excellent. It is drafted in easily understandable and readable form. Besides the excellent pictures of Her Majesty and the Duke of Edinburgh there is an excellent picture of the minister and also one of the undersecretary of state. I have had several people comment on the excellent reports and the clear picture given of the work being done in the dominion archives branch. They show that the work is well organized and that they are doing a lot of work that has not been done up to date.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is a little late to open up a discussion on matters relating to the printing bureau. It is going to take us a while to digest the information we have obtained this evening, so we will cut it short. Initially may I ask the Secretary of State if he can tell us when it is expected the printing bureau will move to its new quarters, and what progress is being made in connection with that building.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that is a subject upon which I am not a very capable prognosticator. It depends on when we can get the steel and when we can proceed with the work. Possibly if my hon. friend were to apply to the Minister of Public Works for information he would get more than I can give him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wonder if the Secretary of State can tell us what is the current rate of wages at the printing bureau.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is $1.75 an hour.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: What is the reason for the large increase in this item?; There is an increase of $281,000. The item is for departmental administration, including in 1952-53 procurement and accounting services to meet stationery and printing requirements for other departments. The amount is $353,732 compared with $72,604 last year, an increase of $281,128. It is four times the amount of the item last year. Why is that increase so pronounced?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The explanation is that in years past a good many of the administrative staff and employees in the printing bureau were paid by a sort of surcharge placed upon the price of work done for the departments through the advance account. This year we are bringing these items into the estimates so it is all before the house.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Does this mean that there is a change in procedure with respect to parliamentary printing? I remember being on the printing committee some years ago, and there was considerable criticism raised about the printing of committee reports. The reports would be printed in English and then months later a contract would be let and the reports would then be printed in French. They were only available months after the session had ended. There was considerable criticism of that practice in the committee because by that time the French version of those committee reports would be virtually
[Mr. Herrldge.l
valueless. They would be out of date. Has that practice been stopped, and does this increase in the estimate take care of that?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: This item brings about no change in the procedure. The reports come out in English first because for the most part the proceedings are in English and they have to be translated into French. That is what causes whatever delay there may be in the production of the French copies of the reports. This item makes no difference in procedure.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The committee reports in French are contracted to printers outside the printing bureau, are they?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Some are and some are not.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Can the minister give me any idea of the percentage of contracts let outside the printing bureau?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: About 65 per cent of the whole went to outside firms last year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: About 65 per cent?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Of the total.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Sixty-five per cent of the total printing went to outside firms? Can the minister give me an idea of the cost of that in round figures?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: About $4J million. That does not include paper. We usually provide the paper.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Printing to the value of $4J million went to outside printers?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The printing bureau provided the paper and the $4J million went to outside firms simply for printing. Is that so?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
That is correct.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
